Chapter 0 Introduction to the Galois Theory of Linear Differential Equations

1 Introduction

This paper is an expanded version of the 10 lectures I gave as the 2006 London Mathematical Society Invited Lecture Series at the Heriot-Watt University, 31 July - 4 August 200611 1 I would like to thank the London Mathematical Society for inviting me to present these lectures, the Heriot-Watt University for hosting them and the International Centre for the Mathematical Sciences for sponsoring a mini-programme on the Algebraic Theory of Differential Equations to complement these talks. Thanks also go to the Edinburgh Mathematical Society and the Royal Society of Edinburgh, who provided support for some of the participants and to Chris Eilbeck, Malcolm MacCallum, and Alexandre Mikhailov for organizing these events. This material is based upon work supported by the National Science Foundation under Grant No. 0096842 and 0634123. My goal was to give the audience an introduction to the algebraic, analytic and algorithmic aspects of the Galois theory of linear differential equations by focusing on some of the main ideas and philosophies and on examples. There are several texts ([Beu92, Kap76, Kol76, Mag94, dPS03] to name a few) that give detailed expositions and I hope that the taste offered here will encourage the reader to dine more fully with one of these.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, What is a Linear Differential Equation?, I discuss three ways to think about linear differential equations: scalar equations, linear systems and differential modules. Just as it is useful to think of linear maps in terms of linear equations, matrices and associated modules, it will be helpful in future sections to go back and forth between the different ways of presenting linear differential equations.

In Section 3, Basic Galois Theory and Applications, I will give the basic definitions and describe the Galois correspondence. In addition I will describe the notion of monodromy and its relation to the Galois theory. I will end by giving several applications and ramifications, one of which will be to answer the question Although y=cos⁡xy=\cos x satisfies y′′+y=0y^{\prime\prime}+y=0, why doesn’t sec⁡x\sec x satisfy a linear differential equation?

In Section 4, Local Galois Theory, I will discuss the formal solution of a linear differential equation at a singular point and describe the asymptotics which allow one to associate with it an analytic solution in a small enough sector at that point. This will involve a discussion of Gevrey asymptotics, the Stokes phenomenon and its relation to the Galois theory. A motivating question (which we will answer in this section) is In what sense does the function

f⁡(x)=∫0∞11+ζ​e−ζx​𝑑ζf(x)=\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{1+\zeta}e^{-\frac{\zeta}{x}}d\zeta

represent the divergent series

∑n≥0(−1)n​n!​xn+1​?\sum_{n\geq 0}(-1)^{n}n!x^{n+1}\ ?

In Section 5, Algorithms, I turn to a discussion of algorithms that allow us to determine properties of a linear differential equation and its Galois group. I will show how category theory, and in particular the tannakian formalism, points us in a direction that naturally leads to algorithms. I will also discuss algorithms to find “closed form solutions” of linear differential equations.

In Section 6, Inverse Problems, I will consider the problem of which groups can appear as Galois groups of linear differential equations. I will show how monodromy and the ideas in Section 4 play a role as well as ideas from Lie theory.

In Section 7, Families of Linear Differential Equations, I will look at linear differential equations that contain parameters and ask How does the Galois group change as we vary the parameters?. This will lead to a discussion of a a generalization of the above theory to a Galois theory of parameterized linear differential equations.

2 What is a Linear Differential Equation?

I will develop an algebraic setting for the study of linear differential equations. Although there are many interesting questions concerning differential equations in characteristic pp [MvdP03a, MvdP03b, dP95, dP96], we will restrict ourselves throughout this paper, without further mention, to fields of characteristic 00. I begin with some basic definitions.

Definition 2.1

1) A differential ring (R,Δ)(R,\Delta) is a ring RR with a set Δ={∂1,…,∂m}\Delta=\{{\partial}_{1},\ldots,{\partial}_{m}\} of maps (derivations) ∂i:R→R{\partial}_{i}:R\rightarrow R, such that

  1. 1.

    ∂i(a+b)=∂i(a)+∂i(b),∂i(a​b)=∂i(a)​b+a​∂i(b){\partial}_{i}(a+b)={\partial}_{i}(a)+{\partial}_{i}(b),\ \ {\partial}_{i}(ab)={\partial}_{i}(a)b+a{\partial}_{i}(b) for all a,b∈Ra,b\in R, and

  2. 2.

    ∂i∂j=∂j∂i{\partial}_{i}{\partial}_{j}={\partial}_{j}{\partial}_{i} for all i,ji,j.

2) The ring CR={c∈R|∂(c)=0∀∂∈Δ}C_{R}=\{c\in R\ |\ {\partial}(c)=0\ \forall\ {\partial}\in\Delta\} is called the ring of constants of RR.

When m=1m=1, we say RR is an ordinary differential ring (R,∂)(R,{\partial}). We frequently use the notation a′a^{\prime} to denote ∂(a){\partial}(a) for a∈Ra\in R. A differential ring that is also a field is called a differential field. If kk is a differential field, then CkC_{k} is also a field.

Examples 2.2

1) (C∞​(ℝm),Δ={∂∂x1,…,∂∂xm}CLOSE(C^{\infty}({\mathbb{R}}^{m}),\Delta=\{\frac{{\partial}}{{\partial}x_{1}},\ldots,\frac{{\partial}}{{\partial}x_{m}}\}) = infinitely differentiable functions on ℝm{\mathbb{R}}^{m}.
2) (ℂ⁡(x1,…,xm),Δ={∂∂x1,…,∂∂xm}CLOSE({\mathbb{C}}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}),\Delta=\{\frac{{\partial}}{{\partial}x_{1}},\ldots,\frac{{\partial}}{{\partial}x_{m}}\}) = field of rational functions
3) (ℂ⁡[[x]],∂∂x)({\mathbb{C}}[[x]],\frac{{\partial}}{{\partial}x}) = ring of formal power series
     ℂ⁡((x))= quotient field of ​ℂ​[[x]]=ℂ⁡[[x]]​[1x]{\mathbb{C}}((x))=\mbox{ quotient field of }{\mathbb{C}}[[x]]={\mathbb{C}}[[x]][\frac{1}{x}]
4) (ℂ​{{x}},∂∂x)({\mathbb{C}}\{\{x\}\},\frac{{\partial}}{{\partial}x}) = ring of germs of convergent series
     ℂ⁡({x})= quotient field of ​ℂ​{{x}}=ℂ​{{x}}​[1x]{\mathbb{C}}(\{x\})=\mbox{ quotient field of }{\mathbb{C}}\{\{x\}\}={\mathbb{C}}\{\{x\}\}[\frac{1}{x}]
5) (ℳ𝒪,Δ={∂∂x1,…,∂∂xm}CLOSE({\mathcal{M}}_{{\mathcal{O}}},\Delta=\{\frac{{\partial}}{{\partial}x_{1}},\ldots,\frac{{\partial}}{{\partial}x_{m}}\}) = field of functions meromorphic on 𝒪open,connected⊂ℂm{\mathcal{O}}^{\rm open,connected}\subset{\mathbb{C}}^{m}

The following result of Seidenberg [Sei58, Sei69] shows that many examples reduce to Example 5) above:

Theorem 2.3

Any differential field kk, finitely generated over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}, is isomorphic to a differential subfield of some ℳ𝒪{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{O}}.

We wish to consider and compare three different versions of the notion of a linear differential equation.

Definition 2.4

Let (k,∂)(k,{\partial}) be a differential field.

  1. 1.

    A scalar linear differential equation is an equation of the form

    L⁡(y)=an​y(n)+…+a0​y=0,ai∈k.L(y)=a_{n}y^{(n)}+\ldots+a_{0}y=0,\ a_{i}\in k.
  2. 2.

    A matrix linear differential equation is an equation of the form

    Y′=A​Y,A∈gln​(k)Y^{\prime}=AY,\ A\in{\rm gl}_{n}(k)

    where gln​(k){\rm gl}_{n}(k) denotes the ring of n×nn\times n matrices with entries in kk.

  3. 3.

    A differential module of dimension nn is an nn-dimensional kk-vector space MM with a map ∂:M→M{\partial}:M\rightarrow M satisfying

    ∂(f​m)=f′​m+f​∂m​ for all ​f∈k,m∈M.{\partial}(fm)=f^{\prime}m+f{\partial}m\mbox{ for all }f\in k,m\in M.

We shall show that these three notions are equivalent and give some further properties.

From scalar to matrix equations: Let L⁡(y)=y(n)+an−1​y(n−1)+…+a0​y=0L(y)=y^{(n)}+a_{n-1}y^{(n-1)}+\ldots+a_{0}y=0. If we let y1=y,y2=y′,…​yn=y(n−1)y_{1}=y,y_{2}=y^{\prime},\ldots y_{n}=y^{(n-1)}, then we have

(y1y2⋮yn−1yn)′=(010…0001…0⋮⋮⋮⋮⋮000…1−a0−a1−a2…−an−1)​(y1y2⋮yn−1yn)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}y_{1}\\ y_{2}\\ \vdots\\ y_{n-1}\\ y_{n}\end{array}\right)^{\prime}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccccc}0&1&0&\ldots&0\\ 0&0&1&\ldots&0\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&1\\ -a_{0}&-a_{1}&-a_{2}&\ldots&-a_{n-1}\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}y_{1}\\ y_{2}\\ \vdots\\ y_{n-1}\\ y_{n}\end{array}\right)

We shall write this last equation as Y′=AL​YY^{\prime}=A_{L}Y and refer ALA_{L} as the companion matrix of the scalar equation and the matrix equation as the companion equation. Clearly any solution of the scalar equation yields a solution of the companion equation and vice versa.
From matrix equations to differential modules (and back):
Given Y′=A​Y,A∈gln​(k)Y^{\prime}=AY,\ A\in{\rm gl}_{n}(k), we construct a differential module in the following way: Let M=kn,e1,…,enM=k^{n},\ e_{1},\ldots,e_{n} the usual basis. Define ∂ei=−∑jaj,iej,{\partial}e_{i}=-\sum_{j}a_{j,i}e_{j}, i.e., ∂e=−At​e{\partial}e=-A^{t}e. Note that if m=∑ifi​eim=\sum_{i}f_{i}e_{i} then ∂m=∑i(fi′−∑jai,j​fj)​ei{\partial}m=\sum_{i}(f_{i}^{\prime}-\sum_{j}a_{i,j}f_{j})e_{i}. In particular, we have that ∂m=0{\partial}m=0 if and only if

(f1⋮fn)′=A⁡(f1⋮fn)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}f_{1}\\ \vdots\\ f_{n}\end{array}\right)^{\prime}=A\left(\begin{array}[]{c}f_{1}\\ \vdots\\ f_{n}\end{array}\right)

It is this latter fact that motivates the seemingly strange definition of this differential module, which we denote by (MA,∂)(M_{A},{\partial}).
Conversely, given a differential module (M,∂)(M,{\partial}), select a basis e=(e1,…,en)e=(e_{1},\ldots,e_{n}). Define AM∈gln​(k)A_{M}\in{\rm gl}_{n}(k) by ∂ei=∑jaj,i​ej{\partial}e_{i}=\sum_{j}a_{j,i}e_{j}. This yields a matrix equation Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY. If e¯=(e¯1,…,e¯n)\bar{e}=(\bar{e}_{1},\ldots,\bar{e}_{n}) is another basis, we get another equation Y′=A¯​YY^{\prime}=\bar{A}Y. If ff and f¯\bar{f} are vectors with respect to these two bases and f=B​f¯,B∈GLn​(k)f=B\bar{f},\ B\in{\rm GL}_{n}(k), then

A¯=B−1​A​B−B−1​B′.\bar{A}=B^{-1}AB-B^{-1}B^{\prime}\ .
Definition 2.5

Let (M1,∂1)(M_{1},{\partial}_{1}) and (M2,∂2)(M_{2},{\partial}_{2}) be differential modules.
1) A differential module homomorphism ϕ:M1→M2\phi:M_{1}\rightarrow M_{2} is a kk-linear map ϕ\phi such that ϕ⁡(∂1(m))=∂2(ϕ⁡(m))\phi({\partial}_{1}(m))={\partial}_{2}(\phi(m)) for all m∈M1m\in M_{1}.
2) The differential modules (M1,∂1)(M_{1},{\partial}_{1}) and (M2,∂1)(M_{2},{\partial}_{1}) are isomorphic if there exists a bijective differential homomorphism ϕ:M1→M2\phi:M_{1}\rightarrow M_{2}.
3) Two differential equations Y′=A1​YY^{\prime}=A_{1}Y and Y′=A2​YY^{\prime}=A_{2}Y are equivalent if the differential modules MA1M_{A_{1}} and MA2M_{A_{2}} are isomorphic

Instead of equivalent, some authors use the term “gauge equivalent” or “of the same type”.
Differential modules offer us an opportunity to study linear differential equations in a basis-free environment. Besides being of theoretical interest, it is important in computations to know that a concept is independent of bases, since this allows one to then select a convenient basis in which to compute.
Before we show how one can recover a scalar equation from a differential module, we show that the standard constructions of linear algebra can be carried over to the context of differential modules. Let (M1,∂1)(M_{1},{\partial}_{1}) and (M2,∂2)(M_{2},{\partial}_{2}) be differential modules and assume that for certain bases these correspond to the equations Y′=A1​YY^{\prime}=A_{1}Y and Y′=A2​YY^{\prime}=A_{2}Y.
In Table 1 we list some standard linear algebra constructions and how they generalize to differential modules. In this table, IniI_{n_{i}} represents the ni×nin_{i}\times n_{i} identity matrix and for two matrices A=(ai,j)A=(a_{i,j}) and BB, A⊗BA\otimes B is the matrix where the i,ji,j-entry of AA is replaced by ai,j​Ba_{i,j}B. Also note that if f∈Homk​(M1,M2)f\in{\rm Hom}_{k}(M_{1},M_{2}) then ∂(f)=0{\partial}(f)=0 if and only if f⁡(∂m1)=∂2(f⁡(m2))f({\partial}m_{1})={\partial}_{2}(f(m_{2})), that is, if and only if ff is a differential module homomorphism.
Referring to the table, it is not hard to show that Homk​(M1,M2)≃M1⊗M2∗{\rm Hom}_{k}(M_{1},M_{2})\simeq M_{1}\otimes M_{2}^{*} as differential modules. Furthermore, given (M,∂)(M,{\partial}) with dimk(M)=n\dim_{k}(M)=n, corresponding to a differential equation Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY, we have that M≃⊕i=1n𝟏kM\simeq\oplus_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbf{1}}_{k}if and only if there exist y1,…,yny_{1},\ldots,y_{n} in knk^{n}, linearly independent over kk such that yi′=A​yiy_{i}^{\prime}=Ay_{i}.

From matrix to scalar linear differential equations: Before I discuss the relationship between matrix and scalar linear differential equations, I need one more concept.

Definition 2.6

Let kk de a differential field. The ring of differential operators over kk = k[∂]k[{\partial}] is the ring of noncommutative polynomials {an∂n+…+a1∂+a0|ai∈k}\{a_{n}{\partial}^{n}+\ldots+a_{1}{\partial}+a_{0}\ |\ a_{i}\in k\} with coeffcients in kk, where multiplication is determined by ∂⋅a=a′+a∂{\partial}\cdot a=a^{\prime}+a{\partial} for all a∈ka\in k.

We shall refer to the degree of an element L∈k[∂]L\in k[{\partial}] as its order o​r​d​L{\mathrm{o}rd}L. The following properties are not hard to check ([dPS03], Chapter 2.1):

Lemma 2.7

Let L1≠0,L2∈k[∂]L_{1}\neq 0,L_{2}\in k[{\partial}].
1) There exist unique Q,R∈k[∂]Q,R\in k[{\partial}] with o​r​d​R<o​r​d​L1{\mathrm{o}rd}R<{\mathrm{o}rd}L_{1} such that L2=Q​L1+RL_{2}=QL_{1}+R.
2) Every left ideal of k[∂]k[{\partial}] is of the form k[∂]Lk[{\partial}]L for some L∈k[∂]L\in k[{\partial}].

We note that any differential module MM can be considered a left k[∂]k[{\partial}]-module and conversely, any left k[∂]k[{\partial}]-module that is finite dimensional as a kk-vector space is a differential module. In fact we have a stronger statement:

Theorem 2.8

(Cyclic Vector Theorem) Assume there exists an a∈ka\in k such that a′≠0a^{\prime}\neq 0. Every differential module is of the form k[∂]/k[∂]Lk[{\partial}]/k[{\partial}]L for some L∈k[∂]L\in k[{\partial}].

This result has many proofs ([CK02, Cop34, Cop36, Del70, Jac37, Kat87a] to name a few), two of which can be found in Chapter 2.1 of [dPS03].

Corollary 2.9

(Systems to Scalar equations) Let kk be as above. Every system Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY is equivalent to a scalar equation L⁡(y)=0L(y)=0.

Proof 2.1.

Let A∗=−AtA^{*}=-A^{t}. Apply the Cyclic Vector Theorem to MA∗M_{A^{*}} to find an L∈k[∂]L\in k[{\partial}] such that MA∗=k[∂]/k[∂]LM_{A^{*}}=k[{\partial}]/k[{\partial}]L. If ALA_{L} is the companion matrix of LL, a calculation shows that MA≃MALM_{A}\simeq M_{A_{L}}.

We note that the hypothesis that kk contain an element aa with a′≠0a^{\prime}\neq 0 is necessary. If the derivation is trivial on kk, then two matrix equations Y′=A1​YY^{\prime}=A_{1}Y and Y′=A2​YY^{\prime}=A_{2}Y are equivalent if and only if the matrices are similar. There exist many examples of matrices not similar to a companion matrtix.
Before we leave (for now) our discussion of the ring k[∂]k[{\partial}], I wish to make two remarks.
First, we can define a map i:k[∂]→k[∂]i:k[{\partial}]\rightarrow k[{\partial}] by i(∑aj∂j)=∑(−1)j∂jaj,i(\sum a_{j}{\partial}^{j})=\sum(-1)^{j}{\partial}^{j}a_{j},. This map is is an involution (i2=i​di^{2}=id). Denoting i⁡(L)=L∗i(L)=L^{*}, we have that (L1​L2)∗=L2∗​L1∗(L_{1}L_{2})^{*}=L_{2}^{*}L_{1}^{*}. The operator L∗L^{*} is referred to as the adjoint of LL. Using the adjoint one sees that there is right euclidean division as well and that every right ideal of k[∂]k[{\partial}] is also principal.
Second, Lemma 2.7.2 allows us to define

Definition 10

Let L1,L2∈k[∂]L_{1},L_{2}\in k[{\partial}].
1) The least common left multiple LCLM(L1,L2L_{1},L_{2}) of L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} is the monic generator of k[∂]L1∩k[∂]L2k[{\partial}]L_{1}\cap k[{\partial}]L_{2}.
2) The greatest common right divisor GCRD(L1,L2L_{1},L_{2}) of L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} is the monic generator of k[∂]L1+k[∂]L2k[{\partial}]L_{1}+k[{\partial}]L_{2}.

A simple modification of the usual euclidean algorithm allows one to find these objects. One can also define least common right multiples and greatest common left divisors using right ideals.
Solutions I will give properties of solutions of scalar and matrix linear differential equations and define the notion of the solutions of a differential module. Let (k,∂)(k,{\partial}) be a differential field with constants CkC_{k} (see Definition 2.1).

Lemma 11.

Let v1,…​vr∈knv_{1},\ldots v_{r}\in k^{n} satisfy vi′=A​viv_{i}^{\prime}=Av_{i}, A∈gln​(k)A\in{\rm gl}_{n}(k). If v1,…,vrv_{1},\ldots,v_{r} are kk-linearly dependent, then they are CkC_{k}-linearly dependent.

Assume, by induction, that v2,…,vrv_{2},\ldots,v_{r} are kk-linearly independent and v1=∑i=2rai​vi,ai∈kv_{1}=\sum_{i=2}^{r}a_{i}v_{i},a_{i}\in k. We then have

0=v1′−A​v1=∑i=2rai′​vi+∑i=2rai​(vi′−A​vi)=∑i=2rai′​vi0=v_{1}^{\prime}-Av_{1}=\sum_{i=2}^{r}a_{i}^{\prime}v_{i}+\sum_{i=2}^{r}a_{i}(v_{i}^{\prime}-Av_{i})=\sum_{i=2}^{r}a_{i}^{\prime}v_{i}

so by assumption, each ai′=0a_{i}^{\prime}=0.

Corollary 12.

Let (k,∂)(k,{\partial}) be a differential field with constants CkC_{k}, A∈gln​(k)A\in{\rm gl}_{n}(k) and L∈k[∂]L\in k[{\partial}].
1) The solution space Solnk​(Y′=A​Y){\rm Soln}_{k}(Y^{\prime}=AY) of Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY in knk^{n} is a CkC_{k}-vector space of dimension at most nn.
2) The elements y1,…,yr∈ky_{1},\ldots,y_{r}\in k are linearly dependent over CkC_{k} if and only if the wronskian determinant

is zero.

1) This follows immediately from Lemma 11.

In general, the dimension of the solutions space of a linear differential equation in a field is less than nn. In the next section we will construct a field such that over this field the solutions space has dimension nn. It will be useful to have the following definition

Definition 13

Let (k,∂)(k,{\partial}) be a differential field, A∈gln​(k)A\in{\rm gl}_{n}(k) and RR a differential ring containing kk. A matrix Z∈GLn​(R)Z\in{\rm GL}_{n}(R) such that Z′=A​ZZ^{\prime}=AZ is called a fundamental solution matrix of Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY.

Note that if RR is a field and ZZ is a fundamental solution matrix, then the columns of ZZ form a CRC_{R}-basis of the solution space of Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY in RR and that this solution space has dimension nn.
Let (M,∂)(M,{\partial}) be a differential module over kk. We define the solution space Solnk​(M){\rm Soln}_{k}(M) of (M,∂)(M,{\partial}) to be the kernel kerM∂\ker_{M}{\partial} of ∂{\partial} on MM. As we have noted above, if {ei}\{e_{i}\} is a basis of MM and Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY is the associated matrix differential equation in this basis, then ∑iviei∈ker∂\sum_{i}v_{i}e_{i}\in\ker{\partial} if and only if v′=A​vv^{\prime}=Av where v=(v1,…,vn)tv=(v_{1},\ldots,v_{n})^{t}. If K⊃kK\supset k is a differential extension of kk, then K⊗kMK\otimes_{k}M can be given the structure of a KK-differential module, where ∂(a⊗m)=a′⊗m+a⊗∂m{\partial}(a\otimes m)=a^{\prime}\otimes m+a\otimes{\partial}m. We then define SolnK​(M){\rm Soln}_{K}(M) to be the kernel ker(∂,K⊗kM)\ker({\partial},K\otimes_{k}M) of ∂{\partial} on K⊗kMK\otimes_{k}M.

3 Basic Galois Theory and Applications

Galois theory of polynomials The idea behind the Galois theory of polynomials is to associate to a polynomial a group (the group of symmetries of the roots that preserve all the algebraic relations among these roots) and deduce properties of the roots from properties of this group (for example, a solvable group implies that the roots can be expressed in terms of radicals). This idea can be formalized in the following way.
Let kk be a field (of characteristic 00 as usual) and let P⁡(X)∈k⁡[X]P(X)\in k[X] be a polynomial of degree nn without repeated roots (i.e., GCD(P.P′)=1{\rm GCD}(P.P^{\prime})=1). Let

S=k⁡[X1,…,Xn,1∏(Xi−Xj)]S=k[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n},\frac{1}{\prod(X_{i}-X_{j})}]

(the reason for the term 1∏(Xi−Xj)\frac{1}{\prod(X_{i}-X_{j})} will be explained below) and let I=(P⁡(X1),…,P⁡(Xn))⊲SI=(P(X_{1}),\ldots,P(X_{n}))\triangleleft S be the ideal generated by the P⁡(Xi)P(X_{i}). The ring S/IS/I is generated by nn distinct roots of PP but does not yet reflect the possible algebraic relations among these roots. We therefore consider any maximal ideal MM in SS containing II. This ideal can be thought of as a maximally consistent set of algebraic relations among the roots. We define

Definition 1

1) The splitting ring of the polynomial PP over kk is the ring

R=S/M=k⁡[X1,…,Xn,1∏(Xi−Xj)]/M.R=S/M=k[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n},\frac{1}{\prod(X_{i}-X_{j})}]/M\ .

2) The Galois group of PP (or of RR over kk) is the group of automorphisms Aut⁡(R/k){\rm Aut}(R/k).

Note that since MM is a maximal ideal, RR is actually a field. Furthermore, since SS contains 1∏(Xi−Xj)\frac{1}{\prod(X_{i}-X_{j})}, the images of the XiX_{i} in RR are distinct roots of PP. So, in fact, RR coincides with the usual notion of a splitting field (a field generated over kk by the distinct roots of PP) and as such, is unique up to kk-isomorphism. Therefore, RR is independent of the choice of maximal ideal MM containing II. We will follow a similar approach with linear differential equations.
Galois theory of linear differential equations Let (k,∂)(k,{\partial}) be a differential field and Y′=A​Y,A∈gln​(k)Y^{\prime}=AY,A\in{\rm gl}_{n}(k) a matrix differential equation over kk. We now want the Galois group to be the group of symmetries of solutions preserving all algebraic and differential relations. We proceed in a way similar to the above.
Let

S=k⁡[Y1,1,…,Yn,n,1det(Yi,j)]S=k[Y_{1,1},\ldots,Y_{n,n},\frac{1}{\det(Y_{i,j})}]

where Y=(Yi,j)Y=(Y_{i,j}) is an n×nn\times n matrix of indeterminates. We define a derivation on SS by setting Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY. The columns of YY form nn independent solutions of the matrix linear differential equation Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY but we have not yet taken into account other possible algebraic and differential relations. To do this, let MM be any maximal differential ideal and let R=S/MR=S/M. We have now constructed a ring that satisfies the following definition

Definition 2

Let (k,∂)(k,{\partial}) be a differential field and Y′=A​Y,A∈gln​(k)Y^{\prime}=AY,A\in{\rm gl}_{n}(k) a matrix differential equation over kk. A Picard-Vessiot ring (PV-ring) for Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY is a differential ring RR over kk such that

  1. 1.

    RR is a simple differential ring (i.e., the only differential ideals are (0)(0) and RR).

  2. 2.

    There exists a fundamental matrix Z∈GLn​(R)Z\in{\rm GL}_{n}(R) for the equation Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY.

  3. 3.

    R is generated as a ring by kk, the entries of ZZ and 1detZ\frac{1}{\det Z}.

One can show that a PV-ring must be a domain and, if CkC_{k} is algebraically closed, then any PV-rings for the same equation are kk-isomorphic as differential rings and Ck=CRC_{k}=C_{R}. Since a PV-ring is a domain we define a PV-field KK to be the quotient field of a PV-ring. Assuming that CkC_{k} is algebraically closed this is the same as saying that KK is generated over kk by the entries of a fundamental solution matrix and that CK=CkC_{K}=C_{k}. These facts are proven in Chapter 1.2 of [dPS03]. From now on, we will always assume that CkC_{k}is algebraically closed (see [Dyc05, HvdP95, Kol76, Ulm94] for results when this is not the case) .

Case 1: α=nm,G​C​D​(n,m)=1\alpha=\frac{n}{m},\ \ GCD(n,m)=1. I claim that ℛ=k⁡[Y,1Y]/[Ym−xn]=k⁡(xmn){\mathcal{R}}=k[Y,\frac{1}{Y}]/[Y^{m}-x^{n}]=k(x^{\frac{m}{n}}). As expected the differential Galois group is defined as

Definition 4

Let (k,∂)(k,{\partial}) be a differential field and RR a PV-ring over kk. The differential Galois group of RR over kk, DGal⁡(R/k){\rm DGal}(R/k) is the group {σ:R→R|σ is a differential k-isomorphism}\{\sigma:R\rightarrow R\ |\ \sigma\mbox{ is a differential $k$-isomorphism}\}.

If RR is the PV-ring associated with Y′=A​Y,A∈gln​(k)Y^{\prime}=AY,A\in{\rm gl}_{n}(k), we sometimes denote the differential Galois group by DGal⁡(Y′=A​Y){\rm DGal}(Y^{\prime}=AY). If KK is a PV-field over kk, then the kk-differential automorphisms of KK over kk are can be identified with the differential kk-automorphisms of RR over kk where RR is a PV-ring whose quotient field is KK.
Let RR be a PV-ring for the equation Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY over kk and σ∈DGal⁡(R/k)\sigma\in{\rm DGal}(R/k). Fix a fundamental solution matrix ZZ and let σ∈DGal⁡(R/k)\sigma\in{\rm DGal}(R/k). We then have that σ⁡(Z)\sigma(Z) is again a fundamental solution matrix of Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY and, a calculation shows that (Z−1​σ​(Z))′=0(Z^{-1}\sigma(Z))^{\prime}=0. Therefore, σ⁡(Z)=Z​mσ\sigma(Z)=Zm_{\sigma} for some mσ∈GLn​(Ck)m_{\sigma}\in{\rm GL}_{n}(C_{k}). This gives an injective group homomorphism σ↦mσ\sigma\mapsto m_{\sigma} of DGal⁡(R/k){\rm DGal}(R/k) into GLn​(Cσ){\rm GL}_{n}(C_{\sigma}). If we select a different fundamental solution matrix, the images of the resulting maps would be conjugate. The image has a further property.

Definition 5

A subgroup GG of GLn​(Ck){\rm GL}_{n}(C_{k}) is said to be a linear algebraic group if it is a Zariski close the zero set in GLn​(Ck){\rm GL}_{n}(C_{k}) of a system of polynomials over CkC_{k} in n2n^{2} variables.

With the identification above DGal⁡(R/k)⊂GLn​(Ck){\rm DGal}(R/k)\subset{\rm GL}_{n}(C_{k}) we have

One can define the differential Galois group of a differential module in the following way. Let MM be a differential module. Once we have selected a basis, we may assume that M≃MAM\simeq M_{A}, where MAM_{A} is the differential module associated with Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY. We say that Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY is a matrix linear differential equation associated with MM.

Definition 8

Let MM be a differential module over kk. The differential Galois group of MM is the differential Galois group of an associated matrix linear differential equation.

To show that this definition makes sense we must show (see the discussion before Definition 2.5) that equivalent matrix differential equations have the same differential Galois groups. Let Y′=A1​YY^{\prime}=A_{1}Y, Y′=A2​YY^{\prime}=A_{2}Y be equivalent equations and let A1=B−1​A2​B−B−1​B′,B∈GLn​(k)A_{1}=B^{-1}A_{2}B-B^{-1}B^{\prime},\ \ B\in{\rm GL}_{n}(k). If R=k⁡[Z1,1Z2]R=k[Z_{1},\frac{1}{Z_{2}}] is a PV-ring for Y′=A1​YY^{\prime}=A_{1}Y, then a computation shows that Z2=B​Z1Z_{2}=BZ_{1} is a fundamental solution matrix for Y′=A2​YY^{\prime}=A_{2}Y and so RR will also be a PV-ring for Y′=A2​YY^{\prime}=A_{2}Y. The equation Z2=B​Z1Z_{2}=BZ_{1} furthermore shows that the action of the differential Galois group (as a matrix group) on Z1Z_{1} and Z2Z_{2} is the same.

We now state

Theorem 9.

(Fundamental Theorem of Differential Galois Theory) Let kk be a differential field with algebraically closed constants CkC_{k}. Let KK be a Picard-Vessiot field with differential Galois group GG.
1) There is a bijective correspondence between Zariski-closed subgroups H⊂GH\subset G and differential subfields FF, k⊂F⊂Kk\subset F\subset K given by

H⊂G\displaystyle H\subset G ↦\displaystyle\mapsto KH={a∈K|σ⁡(a)=a​ for all ​σ∈H}\displaystyle K^{H}=\{a\in K\ |\ \sigma(a)=a\mbox{ for all }\sigma\in H\}
k⊂F⊂K\displaystyle k\subset F\subset K ↦\displaystyle\mapsto DGal⁡(K/F)={σ∈G|σ⁡(a)=a​ for all ​a∈F}\displaystyle{\rm DGal}(K/F)=\{\sigma\in G\ |\ \sigma(a)=a\mbox{ for all }a\in F\}

2) A differential subfield k⊂F⊂Kk\subset F\subset K is a Picard-Vessiot extension of kk if and only if DGal⁡(K/F){\rm DGal}(K/F) is a normal subgroup of GG, in which case DGal⁡(F/k)≃DGal⁡(K/k)​DGal​(K/F){\rm DGal}(F/k)\simeq{\rm DGal}(K/k){\rm DGal}(K/F).

The Zariski closed sets form the collection of closed sets of a topology on GLn{\rm GL}_{n} and one can speak of closures, components, etc. in this topology. In this topology, each linear algebraic group GG may be written (uniquely) as the finite disjoint union of connected closed subsets (see Appendix A of [dPS97] or [Spr98] for a further discussion of linear algebraic groups). The connected component containing the identity matrix is denoted by G0G^{0} and is referred to as the identity component. It is a normal subgroup of GG. As a consequence of the Fundamental Theorem, one can show the folowing:

Corollary 10.

Let k,Kk,K and GG be as above.
1) For a∈Ka\in K, we have that a∈k⇔σ⁡(a)=a​∀σ∈D​G​a​l​(K/k)\ a\in k\Leftrightarrow\sigma(a)=a\ \forall\sigma\in DGal(K/k)
2) For H⊂D​G​a​l​(K/k),H\subset DGal(K/k), the Zariski closure H¯\overline{H} is DGal⁡(K/k){\rm DGal}(K/k) if and only if KH=kK^{H}=k
3) KG0K^{G^{0}} is precisely the algebraic closure k~\tilde{k} of kk in KK.

I refer the reader to Chapter 1.3 of [dPS03] for the proof of the Fundamental Theorem and its corollary.

Galois theory and torsors Let kk be a field (not necessarily a differential field) and k¯\bar{k} its algebraic closure. I wish to refine the notion of a Zariski closed set in order to keep track of the field over which these objects are defined.

Definition 12

1) A Zariski closed subset V⊂k¯nV\subset\bar{k}^{n} is called a variety defined over kk or kk-variety if it the set of common zeroes of polynomials in k⁡[X1,…​Xn]k[X_{1},\ldots X_{n}].
2) If VV is a variety defined over kk, the kk-ideal of VV, Ik​(V),I_{k}(V), is {f∈k⁡[X1,…,Xn]|f⁡(a)=0​ for all ​a∈X}\{f\in k[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]\ |\ f(a)=0\mbox{ for all }a\in X\}.
3) If VV is a variety defined over kk, the kk-coordinate ring, k⁡[V]k[V], of VV is the ring k⁡[X1,…,Xn]/Ik​(V)k[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]/I_{k}(V).
4) If V⊂k¯nV\subset\bar{k}^{n} and W⊂k¯nW\subset\bar{k}^{n}, a kk-morphism f:V→Wf:V\rightarrow W is an nn-tuple of polynomials f=(f1,…,fn)f=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}) in k⁡[X1,…,Xn]k[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}] such that f⁡(a)∈Wf(a)\in W for all a∈Va\in V.
5) We say two kk-varieties VV and WW are kk-isomorphic if there are kk-morphisms f:V→Wf:V\rightarrow W and g:W→Vg:W\rightarrow V such that f​gfg and g​fgf are the identity maps.

Note that the coordinate ring is isomorphic to the ring of kk-morphisms from VV to kk. Also note that a kk-morphism f:V→Wf:V\rightarrow W induces a kk-algebra homomorphism f∗:k⁡[W]→k⁡[V]f^{*}:k[W]\rightarrow k[V] given by f∗​(g)​(v)=g⁡(f⁡(v))f^{*}(g)(v)=g(f(v)) for v∈Vv\in V and g∈k⁡[W]g\in k[W].

Examples 13

1) The affine spaces knk^{n} are ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-varieties and, as such, their coordinate rings are just the rings of polynomials ℚ⁡[X1,…,Xn]{\mathbb{Q}}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}].
2) The group of invertible matrices GLn​(k¯){\rm GL}_{n}(\bar{k}) is also a ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-variety. In order to think of it as a closed set, we must embed each invertible matrix AA in the n+1×n+1n+1\times n+1 matrix (A00det(A))\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}A&0\\ 0&\det(A)\end{array}\right). The defining ideal in ℚ⁡[X1,1,…,Xn+1,n+1]{\mathbb{Q}}[X_{1,1},\ldots,X_{n+1,n+1}] is generated by

Xn+1,1,…,Xn+1,n,X1,n+1,…,Xn,n+1,(detX)−Xn+1,n+1X_{n+1,1},\ldots,X_{n+1,n},X_{1,n+1},\ldots,X_{n,n+1},(\det X)-X_{n+1,n+1}

where XX is the n×nn\times n matrix with entries Xi,j,1≤i≤n,1≤j≤nX_{i,j},1\leq i\leq n,1\leq j\leq n. The coordinate ring is the ring ℚ⁡[X1,1,…,Xn,n,1detX]{\mathbb{Q}}[X_{1,1},\ldots,X_{n,n},\frac{1}{\det X}]

Examples 14

1) Let k=ℚk={\mathbb{Q}} and V={a|a2−2=0}⊂ℚ¯V=\{a\ |\ a^{2}-2=0\}\subset\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}}. We have that Iℚ​(V)=(X2−2)⊂ℚ⁡[X]I_{\mathbb{Q}}(V)=(X^{2}-2)\subset{\mathbb{Q}}[X] and k⁡[V]=ℚ⁡[X]/(X2−2)=ℚ⁡(2)k[V]={\mathbb{Q}}[X]/(X^{2}-2)={\mathbb{Q}}(\sqrt{2}). Note that in this setting “2\sqrt{2}” is a function on VV, defined over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}} with values in ℚ¯\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}} and not a number!
2) Let k=ℚk={\mathbb{Q}} and W={a|a2−1=0}={±1}⊂ℚ¯W=\{a\ |\ a^{2}-1=0\}=\{\pm 1\}\subset\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}}. We have that Iℚ​(W)=(X2−1)I_{\mathbb{Q}}(W)=(X^{2}-1) and k⁡[W]=ℚ⁡[X]/(X2−1)=ℚ⊕ℚk[W]={\mathbb{Q}}[X]/(X^{2}-1)={\mathbb{Q}}\oplus{\mathbb{Q}}.
3) Note that VV and WW are not ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-isomorphic since such an isomorphism would induce an isomorphism of their ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-coordinate rings. If we consider VV and WW as ℚ¯\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}}-varieites, then the map f⁡(x)=(2​(x−1)+2​(x+1))/2f(x)=(\sqrt{2}(x-1)+\sqrt{2}(x+1))/2 gives a ℚ¯\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}}-isomorphism of WW to VV.

We shall be interested in certain kk-subvarieties of GLn​(k¯){\rm GL}_{n}(\bar{k}) that have a group acting on them. These are described in the following definition (a more general definition of torsor is given in Appendix A of [dPS03] but the definition below suffices for our present needs).

Definition 15

Let G⊂GLn​(k¯)G\subset{\rm GL}_{n}(\bar{k}) be a linear algebraic group defined over kk and V⊂GLn​(k¯)V\subset{\rm GL}_{n}(\bar{k}) a kk-variety. We say that VV is a GG-torsor (or GG-principal homogeneous space) over kk if for all v,w∈Vv,w\in V there exists a unique g∈Gg\in G such that v​g=wvg=w. Two GG-torsors V,W∈GLn​(k¯)V,W\in{\rm GL}_{n}(\bar{k}) are said to be kk-isomorphic if there is a kk-isomorphism between the two commuting with the action of GG.

Examples 16

1) GG itself is always a GG-torsor.
2) Let k=ℚk={\mathbb{Q}} and V={a|a2−2=0}⊂ℚ¯V=\{a\ |\ a^{2}-2=0\}\subset\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}}. We have that V⊂ℚ¯∗=GL1​(ℚ¯)V\subset\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}}^{*}={\rm GL}_{1}(\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}}). Let G={±1}⊂GL1​(ℚ¯)G=\{\pm 1\}\subset{\rm GL}_{1}(\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}}). It is easy to see that VV is a GG-torsor. As noted in the previous examples, the torsors VV and GG are not isomorphic over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}} but are isomorphic over ℚ¯\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}}.

We say a GG-torsor over kk is trivial if it is kk-isomorphic to GG itself. One has the following criterion.

Lemma 17.

A GG-torsor VV over kk is trivial if and only if it contains a point with coordinates in kk. In particular, any GG-torsor over an algebraically closed field is trivial.

Proof 3.2.

If VV contains a point vv with coordinates in kk then the map g↦x​gg\mapsto xg is defined over kk and gives a kk-isomorphism between GG and VV (with inverse v↦x−1​vv\mapsto x^{-1}v). If VV is trivial and f:G→Vf:G\rightarrow V is an isomorphism defined over kk, then f⁡(i​d)f(id) has coordinates in kk and so is a kk-point of VV.

For connected groups GG, there are other fields for which all torsors are trivial.

Proposition 18.

Let GG be a connected linear algebraic group defined over kk and VV a GG-torsor over kk. If kk is an algebraic extension of ℂ⁡(x),,ℂ⁡((x)),{\mathbb{C}}(x),\ ,{\mathbb{C}}((x)),or ℂ⁡({x}){\mathbb{C}}(\{x\}), then VV is a trivial GG-torsor.

Proof 3.3.

This result is due to Steinberg, see [Ser64], Chapter III.2.3

Another way of saying that VV is a GG torsor is to say that VV is defined over kk and is a left coset of GG in GLn​(k¯){\rm GL}_{n}(\bar{k}). Because of this one would expect that VV and GG share many geometric properties. The one we will be interested in concerns the dimension. We say that a kk-variety VV is irreducible if it is not the union of two proper kk-varieties. This is equivalent to saying that Ik​(V)I_{k}(V) is a prime ideal or, equivalently, that k⁡[V]k[V] is an integral domain. For an irreducible kk-variety VV, one defines the dimension of VV, dimk(V)\dim_{k}(V) to be the transcendence degree of k⁡(V)k(V) over kk, where k⁡(V)k(V) is the quotient field of k⁡[V]k[V]. For example, if k=ℂk={\mathbb{C}} and VV is a kk-variety that is nonsingular as a complex manifold, then the dimension in the above sense is just the dimension as a complex manifold (this happens for example when VV is a subgroup of GLn​(ℂ){\rm GL}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})). In general, any kk-variety VV can be written as the irredundant union of irreducible kk-varieties, called the irreducible components of VV and the dimension of VV is defined to be the maximum of the dimensions of its irreducible components. One can show that if k⊂Kk\subset K, then dimk(V)=dimK(V)\dim_{k}(V)=\dim_{K}(V) and in particular, dimk(V)=dimk¯V\dim_{k}(V)=\dim_{\bar{k}}V (see [dPS03], Appendix A for more information about kk-varieties).

Proposition 19.

If VV is a GG-torsor, then dimk(V)=dimk(G)\dim_{k}(V)=\dim_{k}(G).

Proof 3.4.

As noted above, any GG-torsor over kk is trivial when considered as a k¯\bar{k} torsor. We therefore have dimk(V)=dimk¯(V)=dimk¯(G)=dimk(G)\dim_{k}(V)=\dim_{\bar{k}}(V)=\dim_{\bar{k}}(G)=\dim_{k}(G).

The reason for introducing the concept of a GG-torsor in this paper is the following proposition. We use the fact that if VV is a GG-torsor over kk and g∈Gg\in G, then the isomorphism ρg:v↦v​g\rho_{g}:v\mapsto vg induces an isomorphism ρg∗:k⁡[V]→k⁡[V]\rho_{g}^{*}:k[V]\rightarrow k[V].

Proposition 20.

Let RR be a Picard-Vessiot extension with differential Galois group GG. Then RR is the coordinate ring of a GG-torsor VV defined over kk. Furthermore, for σ∈G\sigma\in G, the Galois action of σ\sigma on R=k⁡[V]R=k[V] is the same as ρσ∗\rho_{\sigma}^{*}.

Corollary 21.

1) If KK is a Picard-Vessiot field over kk with Galois group GG, then dimCkG=t​r.d​e​g.(K/k)\dim_{C_{k}}G=tr.deg.(K/k).
2) If RR is a Picard-Vessiot ring over kk with Galois group GG where kk is either algebraically closed, ℂ⁡(x),ℂ⁡((x)),{\mathbb{C}}(x),\ {\mathbb{C}}((x)), or ℂ⁡({x}){\mathbb{C}}(\{x\}), then R≃k⁡[G]R\simeq k[G].

We refer to Chapter 1.3 of [dPS03] for a proof of the proposition and note that the Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory is shown there to follow from this proposition.

Another application concerning solving linear differential equations in terms of special functions and algorithms to do this will be discussed in Section 5. The Picard-Vessiot theory has also been used to identify obstructions to complete integrability of Hamiltonian systems (see [Aud01] or [MR99])
Monodromy. We will now consider differential equations over the complex numbers, so let k=ℂ⁡(x),x′=1k={\mathbb{C}}(x),\ x^{\prime}=1 and

d​Yd​x\displaystyle\frac{dY}{dx} =\displaystyle= A⁡(x)​Y,A⁡(x)∈gln​(ℂ⁡(x))\displaystyle A(x)Y,\ A(x)\in{\rm gl}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}(x)) (1)
Definition 22

A point x0∈ℂx_{0}\in{\mathbb{C}} is an ordinary point of equation (1) if all the entries of A⁡(x)A(x) are analytic at x0x_{0}, otherwise x0x_{0} is a singular point.

One can also consider the point at infinity, ∞\infty. Let t=1xt=\frac{1}{x}. We then have that d​Yd​t=−1t2​A​(1t)​Y\frac{dY}{dt}=-\frac{1}{t^{2}}A(\frac{1}{t})Y. The point x=∞x=\infty is an ordinary or singular point precisely when t=0t=0 is an ordinary or singular point of the transformed equation.

Example 23

d​yd​x=αx​y⇒d​yd​t=−αt​y\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{\alpha}{x}y\Rightarrow\frac{dy}{dt}=-\frac{\alpha}{t}y so the singular points are {0,∞}\{0,\infty\}.

Let S=ℂ​ℙ1S={\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{1} be the Riemann Sphere and let X=S2−{singular points of (1)}X=S^{2}-\{\mbox{singular points of (\ref{eqnmono})}\} and let x0∈Xx_{0}\in X. From standard existence theorems, we know that in a small neighborhood 𝒪{\mathcal{O}} of x0x_{0}, there exists a fundamental matrix ZZ whose entries are analytic in 𝒪{\mathcal{O}}. Let γ\gamma be a closed curve in XX based at x0x_{0}. Analytic continuation along γ\gamma yields a new fundamental solution matrix ZγZ_{\gamma} at x0x_{0} which must be related to the old fundamental matrix as

Zγ\displaystyle Z_{\gamma} =\displaystyle= Z​Dγ\displaystyle ZD_{\gamma}

where Dγ∈GLn​(ℂ)D_{\gamma}\in{\rm GL}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}). One can show that DγD_{\gamma} just depends on the homotopy class of γ\gamma. This defines a homomorphism

Mon:π1​(X,x0)\displaystyle{\rm Mon}:\pi_{1}(X,x_{0}) →\displaystyle\rightarrow GLn​(ℂ)\displaystyle{\rm GL}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})
γ\displaystyle\gamma ↦\displaystyle\mapsto Dγ\displaystyle D_{\gamma}
Definition 24

The homomorphism Mon{\rm Mon} is called the monodromy map and its image is called the monodromy group.

Note that the monodromy group depends on the choice of ZZ so it is only determined up to conjugation. Since analytic continuation preserves analytic relations, we have that the monodromy group is contained in the differential Galois group.

Examples 25

1) y′=αx​y(y=eα​log⁡x=xα)y^{\prime}=\frac{\alpha}{x}y\ \ (y=e^{\alpha\log x}=x^{\alpha}) Singular points = {0,∞}\{0,\infty\}

Mon⁡(π1​(X,x0))={(e2​π​i​α)n|n∈ℤ}{\rm Mon}(\pi_{1}(X,x_{0}))=\{(e^{2\pi i\alpha})^{n}\ |\ n\in{\mathbb{Z}}\}

If α∈ℚ\alpha\in{\mathbb{Q}} this image is finite and so equals the differential Galois group. If α∉ℚ\alpha\notin{\mathbb{Q}}, then this image is infinite and so Zariski dense in GL1​(ℂ){\rm GL}_{1}({\mathbb{C}}). In either case the monodromy group is Zariski dense in the differential Galois group.
2) y′=y(y=ex)y^{\prime}=y\ \ (y=e^{x}), Singular points = {∞}\{\infty\}

Mon⁡(π1​(X,x0))={1}{\rm Mon}(\pi_{1}(X,x_{0}))=\{1\}

In this example the differential Galois group is GL1​(ℂ){\rm GL}_{1}({\mathbb{C}}) and the monodromy group is not Zariski dense in this group.

The second example shows that the monodromy group is not necessarily Zariski dense in the differential Galois group but the first example suggests that under certain conditions it may be. To state these conditions we need the following defintions.

Definition 26

1) An open sector 𝒮=𝒮⁡(a,b,ρ){\mathcal{S}}={\mathcal{S}}(a,b,\rho) at a point pp is the set of complex numbers z≠pz\neq p such that arg⁡(z−p)∈(a,b)\arg(z-p)\in(a,b) and |z−p|<ρ⁡(arg⁡(z−p))|z-p|<\rho(\arg(z-p)) where ρ:(a,b)→ℝ>0\rho:(a,b)\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}_{>0} is a continuous function.
2) A singular point pp of Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY is a regular singular point if for any open sector 𝒮⁡(a,b,ρ){\mathcal{S}}(a,b,\rho) at pp with |a−b|<2​π|a-b|<2\pi, there exists a fundamental solution matrix Z=(zi​j)Z=(z_{ij}), analytic in 𝒮{\mathcal{S}} such that for some positive constant cc and integer NN, |zi​j|<c​|xN||z_{ij}|<c|x^{N}| as x→px\rightarrow p in 𝒮{\mathcal{S}}.

Note that in the first example above, the singular points are regular while in the second they are not. For scalar linear differential equations L⁡(y)=y(n)+an−1​y(n−1)+…+a0​y=0L(y)=y^{(n)}+a_{n-1}y^{(n-1)}+\ldots+a_{0}y=0, the criterion of Fuchs states that pp is a regular singular point if and only if each aia_{i} has a pole of order ≤n−i\leq n-i at pp (see Chapter 5.1 of [dPS03] for a further discussion of regular singular points). For equations with only regular singular points we have

Proposition 27.

(Schlesinger) If Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY has only regular singular points, then Mon⁡(π1​(X,x0)){\rm Mon}(\pi_{1}(X,x_{0})) is Zariski dense in D​G​a​lDGal.

Proof 3.5.

Let KK = PV extension field of kk for Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY. We have M​o​n​(π1​(X,x0))⊂D​G​a​l​(K/k)Mon(\pi_{1}(X,x_{0}))\subset DGal(K/k). By Corollary 10 it is enough to show that if f∈Kf\in K is left fixed by M​o​n​(π1​(X,x0))Mon(\pi_{1}(X,x_{0})) then f∈k=ℂ⁡(x)f\in k={\mathbb{C}}(x). If ff is left invariant by analytic continuation on XX, then ff is a single valued meromorphic function on XX. Let Z=(zi​j),zi​j∈KZ=(z_{ij}),z_{ij}\in K be a fundamental solution matrix and let f∈ℂ⁡(x,zi​j)f\in{\mathbb{C}}(x,z_{ij}). Regular singular points imply that ff has polynomial growth near the singular points of Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY and is at worst meromorphic at other points on the Riemann Sphere. Cauchy’s Theorem implies that ff is meromorphic on the Riemann Sphere and Liouville’s Theorem implies that ff must be a rational function.

In Section 4, we shall see what other analytic information one needs to determine the differential Galois group in general.

Factorization of linear differential operators. In Section 5, we will see that factorization properties of linear differential operators and differential modules play a crucial role in algorithms to calculate properties of Galois groups. Here I shall relate factorization of operators to the Galois theory.

Transcendental numbers. Results of Siegel and Shidlovski (and subsequent authors) reduce the problem of showing that the values of certain functions are algebraically independent to showing that these functions are themselves algebraically independent. The Galois theory of linear differential equations can be used to do this.

Definition 29

f=∑i=0∞an​znn!∈ℚ⁡[[z]]f=\sum^{\infty}_{i=0}a_{n}\frac{z^{n}}{n!}\in{\mathbb{Q}}[[z]] is an E-function if ∃c∈ℚ\exists\ c\in{\mathbb{Q}} such that, for all nn, |an|≤cn|a_{n}|\leq c^{n} and the least common denominator of a0,…,an≤cna_{0},\ldots,a_{n}\leq c^{n}.

Examples 30

ex=∑znn!e^{x}=\sum\frac{z^{n}}{n!}, J0​(z)=∑z2​n(n!)2J_{0}(z)=\sum\frac{z^{2n}}{(n!)^{2}}

Theorem 31.

(Siegel-Shidlovski, c.f., [Lan66]): If f1,…,fsf_{1},\ldots,f_{s} are E-functions, algebraically independent over ℚ⁡(z){\mathbb{Q}}(z) and satisfy a linear differential equation

L⁡(y)=y(m)+am−1​y(n−1)+…+a0​y,ai∈ℚ⁡(z)L(y)=y^{(m)}+a_{m-1}y^{(n-1)}+\ldots+a_{0}y,\ \ \ a_{i}\in{\mathbb{Q}}(z)

then for α∈ℚ,α≠0\alpha\in{\mathbb{Q}},\alpha\neq 0 and α\alpha not a pole of the aia_{i}, the numbers f1​(α),…,fs​(α)f_{1}(\alpha),\ldots,f_{s}(\alpha) are algebraically independent over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}.

The differential Galois group of L⁡(y)=0L(y)=0 measures the algebraic relations among solutions. In particular, Corollary 21 implies that if y1,…​yny_{1},\ldots y_{n} are a ℚ¯\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}}-basis of the solution space of L⁡(y)=0L(y)=0 then the transcendence degree of ℚ¯​(x)​(y1,…​yn,y1′,…​yn′,…,y1(n−1),…,yn(n−1))\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}}(x)(y_{1},\ldots y_{n},y_{1}^{\prime},\ldots y_{n}^{\prime},\ldots,y_{1}^{(n-1)},\ldots,y_{n}^{(n-1)}) over ℚ¯​(x)\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}}(x) is equal to the dimension of the differential Galois group of L⁡(y)=0L(y)=0.

Example 32

The differential Galois group of the Bessel equations y′′+1z​y′+(1−λ2z2)​y=0,λ−12∉ℤy^{\prime\prime}+\frac{1}{z}y^{\prime}+(1-\frac{\lambda^{2}}{z^{2}})y=0,\ \lambda-\frac{1}{2}\notin{\mathbb{Z}} over ℚ¯​(x)\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}}(x) can be shown to be SL2{\rm SL}_{2} ([Kol68]) and examining the recurrence defining a power series solution of this equation, one sees that the solutions are E-functions. Given a fundamental set of solutions {Jλ,Yλ}\{J_{\lambda},Y_{\lambda}\} we have that the transcendence degree of ℚ¯​(x)​(Jλ,Yλ,Jλ′,Yλ′)\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}}(x)(J_{\lambda},Y_{\lambda},J_{\lambda}^{\prime},Y_{\lambda}^{\prime}) over ℚ¯​(x)\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}}(x) is 33 (one can show that Jλ​Yλ′−Jλ′,Yλ∈ℚ¯​(x)J_{\lambda}Y_{\lambda}^{\prime}-J_{\lambda}^{\prime},Y_{\lambda}\in\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}}(x). Therefore one can apply the Siegel-Shidlovski Theorem to show that certain values of Jλ,YλJ_{\lambda},Y_{\lambda} and Jλ′J_{\lambda}^{\prime} are algebraically independent over ℚ¯\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}}.

Why does cos⁡x\cos x satisfy a linear differential equation over ℂ⁡(x){\mathbb{C}}(x), while sec⁡x\sec x does not? There are many reasons for this. For example, sec⁡x=1c​o​s​x\sec x=\frac{1}{cosx} has an infinite number of poles which is impossible for a solution of a linear differential equation over ℂ⁡(x){\mathbb{C}}(x). The following result, originally due to Harris and Sibuya [HS85], also yields this result and can be proven using differential Galois theory [Sin86].

Proposition 33.

Let kk be a differential field with algebraically closed constants and KK a PV -field of kk. Assume y≠0,1/y∈Ky\neq 0,1/y\in K satisfy linear differential equations over kk. The y′y\frac{y^{\prime}}{y} is algebraic over kk.

Proof 3.7.

(Outline) We may assume that kk is algebraically closed and that KK is the quotient field of a PV-ring RR. Corollary 21 implies that R=k⁡[G]R=k[G] where GG is an algebraic group whose CkC_{k} points form the Galois group of RR over kk. Since both yy and 1y\frac{1}{y} satisfy linear differential equations over kk, their orbits under the action of the Galois group span a finite dimensional vector space over CkC_{k}. This in turn implies the orbit of that yy and 1y\frac{1}{y} induced by the the action of G⁡(k)G(k) on G⁡(k)G(k) by right multiplication is finite dimensional. The general theory of linear algebraic groups [Spr98] tells us that this implies that these elements must lie in k⁡[G]k[G]. A result of Rosenlicht [Mag76, Ros61] implies that y=a​fy=af where a∈ka\in k and f∈k⁡[G]f\in k[G] satisfies f⁡(g​h)=f⁡(g)​f​(h)f(gh)=f(g)f(h) for all g,h∈Gg,h\in G. In particular, for σ∈G⁡(Ck)=Aut⁡(K/k)\sigma\in G(C_{k})={\rm Aut}(K/k), we have σ⁡(f⁡(x))=f⁡(x​σ)=f⁡(x)​f​(σ)\sigma(f(x))=f(x\sigma)=f(x)f(\sigma). If L∈k[∂]L\in k[{\partial}] is of minimal positive order such that L⁡(f)=0L(f)=0, then 0=σ⁡(L⁡(f))=L⁡(f⋅f⁡(σ))0=\sigma(L(f))=L(f\cdot f(\sigma)) and a calculation shows that this implies that f⁡(σ)∈Ckf(\sigma)\in C_{k}.
We therefore have that, for all σ∈Aut⁡(K/k)\sigma\in{\rm Aut}(K/k) there exists a cσ∈Ckc_{\sigma}\in C_{k} such that σ⁡(y)=cσ​y\sigma(y)=c_{\sigma}y. This implies that y′y\frac{y^{\prime}}{y} is left fixed by Aut⁡(K/k){\rm Aut}(K/k) and so must be in kk.

If y=cos⁡xy=\cos x and 1y=sec⁡x\frac{1}{y}=\sec x both satisfy linear differential equations over ℚ¯​(x)\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}}(x), then the above result implies that tan⁡x\tan x would be algebraic over ℚ¯​(x)\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}}(x). One can show that this is not the case by noting that a periodic function that is algebraic over ℚ¯​(x)\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}}(x) must be constant, a contradiction. Another proof can be given by startng with a putative minimal polynomial P​(Y)∈ℂ​(x)​[Y]P(Y)\in{\mathbb{C}}(x)[Y] and noting that d​Pd​x+d​Pd​Y​Y′=d​Pd​x+d​Pd​Y​(Y2+1)\frac{dP}{dx}+\frac{dP}{dY}Y^{\prime}=\frac{dP}{dx}+\frac{dP}{dY}(Y^{2}+1) must be divisible by PP. Comparing coefficients, one sees that the coefficients of powers of YY must be constant and so tan⁡x\tan x would be constant.
Systems of linear partial differential equations. Let (k,Δ={∂1,…,∂m})(k,\Delta=\{{\partial}_{1},\ldots,{\partial}_{m}\}) be a partial differential field. One can define the ring of linear partial differential operators k[∂1,…,∂m]k[{\partial}_{1},\ldots,{\partial}_{m}] as the noncommutative polynomial ring in ∂1,…,∂m{\partial}_{1},\ldots,{\partial}_{m} where ∂i⋅a=∂i(a)+a∂i{\partial}_{i}\cdot a={\partial}_{i}(a)+a{\partial}_{i} for all a∈ka\in k. In this context, a differential module is a finite dimensional kk-space that is a left k[∂1,…,∂m]k[{\partial}_{1},\ldots,{\partial}_{m}]-module. We have

Proposition 34.

Assume kk contains an element aa such that ∂i(a)≠0{\partial}_{i}(a)\neq 0 for some ii. There is a correspondence between

  • •

    differential modules,

  • •

    left ideals I⊂k[∂1,…,∂m]I\subset k[{\partial}_{1},\ldots,{\partial}_{m}] such that dimkk[∂1,…,∂m]/I<∞\dim_{k}k[{\partial}_{1},\ldots,{\partial}_{m}]/I<\infty, and

  • •

    systems ∂iY=AiY,A∈gln(k),i=1,…m{\partial}_{i}Y=A_{i}Y,A\in{\rm gl}_{n}(k),i=1,\ldots m such that

    ∂i(Aj)+Ai​Aj=∂j(Ai)+Aj​Ai{\partial}_{i}(A_{j})+A_{i}A_{j}={\partial}_{j}(A_{i})+A_{j}A_{i}

    i.e., integrable systems

If

∂iY=AiY,A∈gln(k),i=1,…m{\partial}_{i}Y=A_{i}Y,A\in{\rm gl}_{n}(k),i=1,\ldots m

is an integrable system, the solution space over any differential field is finite dimensional over constants. Furthermore, one can define PV extensions, differential Galois groups, etc. for such systems and develop a Galois theory whose groups are linear algebraic groups. For further details see [Kol76, CS06] and Appendix D of [dPS03].

4 Local Galois Theory

In the previous section, we showed that for equations with only regular singular points the analytically defined monodromy group determines the differential Galois group. In this section we shall give an idea of what analytic information determines the Galois group for general singular points. We shall use the following notation:

    ℂ⁡[[x]]={∑i=0∞ai​xi|ai∈ℂ},x′=1{{\mathbb{C}}[[x]]}=\{\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}a_{i}x^{i}\ |\ a_{i}\in{\mathbb{C}}\},\ \ x^{\prime}=1

    ℂ⁡((x)){{\mathbb{C}}((x))} = quotient field of ℂ⁡[[x]]{\mathbb{C}}[[x]] = ℂ​[[x]]​[x−1]{\mathbb{C}}[[x]][x^{-1}]

  • •

Ordinary points. We say that x=0x=0 is an ordinary point of equation (2) if A∈gln​(ℂ⁡[[x]])A\in{\rm gl}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}[[x]]). The standard existence theory (see [Poo60] for a classical introduction or [Har64]) yields the following:

This implies that for ordinary points with A∈gln​(k)A\in{\rm gl}_{n}(k) where k=ℂ⁡({x})k={\mathbb{C}}(\{x\}) or ℂ⁡((x)){\mathbb{C}}((x)), the Galois group of the associated Picard-Vessiot extension over kk is trivial. The next case to consider is

We now turn to the Galois groups. We first consider the Galois group of a regular singular equation over ℂ⁡({x}){\mathbb{C}}(\{x\}). Let 𝒪{\mathcal{O}} be a connected open neighborhood of 00 such that the entries of AA are regular in 𝒪{\mathcal{O}} with at worst a pole at 00. Let x0≠0x_{0}\neq 0 be a point of 𝒪{\mathcal{O}} and γ\gamma a simple loop around 00 in 𝒪{\mathcal{O}} based at x0x_{0}. There exists a fundamental solution matrix ZZ at x0x_{0} and the field K=k⁡(Z,1detZ)K=k(Z,\frac{1}{\det Z}), k=ℂ⁡({x})k={\mathbb{C}}(\{x\}) is a Picard-Vessiot extension of kk. Analytic continuation around γ\gamma gives a new fundamental solution matrix Zγ=Z​MγZ_{\gamma}=ZM_{\gamma} for some Mγ∈GLn​(ℂ)M_{\gamma}\in{\rm GL}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}). The matrix MγM_{\gamma} depends on the choice of ZZ and so is determined only up to conjugation. Nonetheless, it is referred to as the monodromy matrix at 00. As in our discussion of monodromy in Section 5, we see that MγM_{\gamma} is in the differential Galois group DGal⁡(K/k){\rm DGal}(K/k) and, arguing as in Proposition 27, one sees that MγM_{\gamma} generates a cyclic group that is Zariski dense in DGal⁡(K/k){\rm DGal}(K/k). From the theory of linear algebraic groups, one can show that a linear algebraic group have a Zariski dense cyclic subgroup must be of the form (ℂ∗,×)r×(ℂ,+)s×ℤ/m​ℤ,r≥0,s∈{0,1}({\mathbb{C}}^{*},\times)^{r}\times({\mathbb{C}},+)^{s}\times{\mathbb{Z}}/m{\mathbb{Z}},\ r\geq 0,\ s\in\{0,1\} and that any such group occurs as a differential Galois group of a regular singular equation over kk. (Exercise 5.3 of [dPS03]). This is not too surprising since property (vi) of the above proposition shows that KK is contained in a field of the form k⁡(xα1,…,xαr,log⁡x)k(x^{\alpha_{1}},\ldots,x^{\alpha_{r}},\log x) for some αi∈ℂ\alpha_{i}\in{\mathbb{C}}.
Since ℂ⁡({x})⊂ℂ⁡((x))=k~{\mathbb{C}}(\{x\})\subset{\mathbb{C}}((x))=\tilde{k}, we can consider the the field K~=k~​(Z,1detZ)\tilde{K}=\tilde{k}(Z,\frac{1}{\det Z}) where ZZ is as above. Again, using (vi) above, we have that K~⊂F=k~​(xα1,…,xαr,log⁡x)\tilde{K}\subset F=\tilde{k}(x^{\alpha_{1}},\ldots,x^{\alpha_{r}},\log x) for some αi∈ℂ\alpha_{i}\in{\mathbb{C}}. Since we are no longer dealing with analytic functions, we cannot appeal to analytic continuation but we can define a formal monodromy, that is a differential automorphism of FF over k~\tilde{k} that sends xα↦xα​e2​π​i​αx^{\alpha}\mapsto x^{\alpha}e^{2\pi i\alpha} and log⁡x↦log⁡x+2​π​i\log x\mapsto\log x+2\pi i. One can show that the only elements of FF that are left fixed by this automorphism lie in k~\tilde{k}. This automorphism restricts to an automorphism of K~\tilde{K}. Therefore the Fundamental Theorem implies that the group generated by the formal monodromy is Zariski dense in the differential Galois group DGal⁡(K~/k~){\rm DGal}(\tilde{K}/\tilde{k}). The restriction of the formal monodromy to KK (as above) is just the usual monodromy, so one sees that the convergent Galois group DGal⁡(K/k){\rm DGal}(K/k) equals the formal Galois group DGal⁡(K~/k~){\rm DGal}(\tilde{K}/\tilde{k}).
We note that the existence of nn linearly independent solutions of the form described in (vi) goes back to Fuchs in the 19t​h19^{th} Century and can be constructed using the Frobenius method (see [Gra00] for an historical account of the development of linear differential equations in the 19t​h19^{th} Century).
Irregular singular points. We say x=0x=0 is an irregular singular point if it is not ordinary or regular. Fabry, in the 19t​h19^{th} Century constructed a fundamental set of formal solutions of a scalar linear differential equation at an irregular singular point. In terms of linear systems, every equation of the form Y′=A​Y,A∈gln​(ℂ⁡((x)))Y^{\prime}=AY,\ A\in{\rm gl}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}((x))) has a fundamental solution matrix of the form

Y^=ϕ^​(t)​xL​eQ⁡(1/t)\hat{Y}=\hat{\phi}(t)x^{L}e^{Q(1/t)}

where

  • •

    tν=x,ν∈{1,2,3,…,n!}t^{\nu}=x,\ \nu\in\{1,2,3,\ldots,n!\}

  • •

    ϕ^​(t)∈GLn​(ℂ⁡((t)))\hat{\phi}(t)\in{\rm GL}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}((t)))

  • •

    L∈gln​(ℂ)L\in{\rm gl}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})

    Q=diag⁡(q1,…,qn),qi∈1t​ℂ​[1t]Q={\rm diag}(q_{1},\ldots,q_{n}),q_{i}\in\frac{1}{t}{\mathbb{C}}[\frac{1}{t}]

  • •

    LL and QQ commute.

One refers to the integer ν\nu as the ramification at 00 and the polynomial qiq_{i} as the eigenvalues at 00 of the equation. We note that even if A∈gln​(ℂ⁡({x}))A\in{\rm gl}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}(\{x\})), the matrix ϕ^​(t)\hat{\phi}(t) does not necessarily lie in gln​(ℂ​({t})){\rm gl}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}(\{t\})). There are various ways to make this representation unique but we will not deal with this here. We also note that by adjusting the term xLx^{L}, we can always assume that no ramification occurs in ϕ^​(t)\hat{\phi}(t), that is, ϕ^∈GLn​(ℂ⁡((x)))\hat{\phi}\in{\rm GL}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}((x))) (but one may lose the last commutativity property above). As in the regular case, there are algorithms to determine a fundamental matrix of this form. We refer to Chapter 3 of [dPS03] for a detailed discussion of the existence of these formal solutions and algorithms to calculate them and p. 98 of [dPS03] for historical references and references to some recent work.
I will now give two examples (taken from [LR95]).

Let KK be the Picard-Vessiot extension of ℂ⁡((x)){\mathbb{C}}((x)) for d​Y0d​x=A0​Y0\frac{dY_{0}}{dx}=A_{0}Y_{0} (and therefore also for d​Yd​x=A​Y\frac{dY}{dx}=AY). We have that

The differential Galois group of Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY over ℂ⁡((x)){\mathbb{C}}((x)) is the Zariski closure of the group generated by the formal monodromy and the exponential torus.

One can furthermore show (Proposition 3.25 of [dPS03]) that x=0x=0 is a regular singular point if and only if the exponential torus is trivial.

D​G​a​l​(K/ℂ⁡((x)))=D∞={(c00c−1)|c≠0}∪{(0c−c−10)|c≠0}DGal(K/{\mathbb{C}}((x)))=D_{\infty}=\{\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}c&0\\ 0&c^{-1}\end{array}\right)\ |\ c\neq 0\}\cup\{\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&c\\ -c^{-1}&0\end{array}\right)\ |\ c\neq 0\}

Galois Group over ℂ⁡({x}){\mathbb{C}}(\{x\}): the Convergent Galois Group at x=0x=0. We now assume that we are considering a differential equation with d​Yd​x=A​Y\frac{dY}{dx}=AY with A∈ℂ⁡({x})A\in{\mathbb{C}}(\{x\}) and we let KK be the Picard-Vessiot extension of ℂ⁡({x}){\mathbb{C}}(\{x\}) for this equation. Since ℂ⁡({x})⊂ℂ⁡((x)){\mathbb{C}}(\{x\})\subset{\mathbb{C}}((x)), we have that the formal Galois group DGal⁡(K/ℂ⁡((x))){\rm DGal}(K/{\mathbb{C}}((x))) is a subgroup of the convergent Galois group DGal⁡(K/ℂ⁡({x})){\rm DGal}(K/{\mathbb{C}}(\{x\})). If x=0x=0 is a regular singular point then these Galois groups are the same but in general the convergent group is larger than the formal group. I will describe analytic objects that measure the difference. The basic idea is the following. We have a formal solution Y^=ϕ^​(x)​xL​eQ⁡(1/t)\hat{Y}=\hat{\phi}(x)x^{L}e^{Q(1/t)} for the differential equation. For each small enough sector 𝒮{\mathcal{S}} at x=0x=0 we can give the terms xLx^{L} and eQ⁡(1/t)e^{Q(1/t)} meaning in an obvious way. The matrix ϕ^​(x)\hat{\phi}(x) is a little more problematic but it has been shown that one can find a matrix Φ𝒮\Phi_{\mathcal{S}} of functions, analytic is 𝒮{\mathcal{S}}, “asymptotic” to ϕ^​(x)\hat{\phi}(x) and such that Φ𝒮​(x)​xL​eQ⁡(1/t)\Phi_{\mathcal{S}}(x)x^{L}e^{Q(1/t)} satisfies the differential equation. In overlapping sectors 𝒮1{\mathcal{S}}_{1} and 𝒮2{\mathcal{S}}_{2} the corresponding Φ𝒮1\Phi_{{\mathcal{S}}_{1}} and Φ𝒮2\Phi_{{\mathcal{S}}_{2}} may not agree but they will satisfy Φ𝒮1=Φ𝒮2​S​t12\Phi_{{\mathcal{S}}_{1}}=\Phi_{{\mathcal{S}}_{2}}St_{12} for some S​t12∈GLn​(ℂ)St_{12}\in{\rm GL}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}). The S​ti,jSt_{i,j} ranging over a suitable choice of small sectors 𝒮ℓ{\mathcal{S}}_{\ell} together with the formal Galois group should generate a group that is Zariski dense in the convergent Galois group. There are two (related) problems with this idea. The first is what do we mean by asymptotic and the second is how do we select the sectors and the Φℓ\Phi_{\ell} in some canonical way? We shall first consider these questions for fairly general formal series and then specialize to the situation where the series are entries of matrices ϕ^​(x)\hat{\phi}(x) that arise in the formal solutions of linear differential equations.
Asymptotics and Summability. In the 19t​h19^{th} century, Poincaré proposed the following notion of an asymptotic expansion.

Definition 12

Let ff be analytic on a sector 𝒮=𝒮⁡(a,b,ρ){\mathcal{S}}={\mathcal{S}}(a,b,\rho) at x=0x=0. The series ∑n≥n0cn​xn\sum_{n\geq n_{0}}c_{n}x^{n} is an asymptotic expansion of ff if ∀N≥0\forall N\geq 0 and every closed sector W⊂𝒮W\subset{\mathcal{S}} there exists a constant C⁡(N,W)C(N,W) such that

|f⁡(x)−∑n0≤n≤N−1cn​xn|≤C⁡(N,W)​|x|N∀x∈W.|f(x)-\sum_{n_{0}\leq n\leq N-1}c_{n}x^{n}|\leq C(N,W)|x|^{N}\ \ \forall x\in W.

A function ff analytic on a sector can have at most one asymptotic expansion on that sector and we write J⁡(f)J(f) for this series if it exists. We denote by 𝒜⁡(𝒮⁡(a,b,ρ)){\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{S}}(a,b,\rho)) the set of functions analytic on 𝒮⁡(a,b,ρ){\mathcal{S}}(a,b,\rho) having asymptotic expansions on this sector. We define 𝒜⁡(a,b){\mathcal{A}}(a,b) to be the direct limit of the 𝒜⁡(𝒮⁡(a,b,ρ)){\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{S}}(a,b,\rho)) over all ρ\rho (here we say f1∈𝒜⁡(𝒮⁡(a,b,ρ1))f_{1}\in{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{S}}(a,b,\rho_{1})) and f2∈𝒜⁡(𝒮⁡(a,b,ρ2))f_{2}\in{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{S}}(a,b,\rho_{2})) are equivalent if the agree on the intersection of the sectors). If one thinks of a,b∈S1a,b\in S^{1}, the unit circle, then one can see that the sets 𝒜⁡(a,b){\mathcal{A}}(a,b) form a sheaf on S1S^{1}. We have the following facts (whose proofs can be found in Chapters 7.1 and 7.2 of [dPS03] or in [Bal94]).

  • •

    𝒜⁡(a,b){\mathcal{A}}(a,b) is a differential ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-algebra.

  • •

    𝒜⁡(S1)=ℂ⁡({x}){\mathcal{A}}(S^{1})={\mathbb{C}}(\{x\}).

  • •

    (Borel-Ritt) For all (a,b)≠S1(a,b)\neq S^{1}, the map J:𝒜⁡(a,b)→ℂ⁡((x))J:{\mathcal{A}}(a,b)\rightarrow{\mathbb{C}}((x)) is surjective.

Given a power series in ℂ⁡((x)){\mathbb{C}}((x)) that satisfies a linear differential equation, one would like to say that it is the asymptotic expansion of an analytic function that also satisfies the differential equation. Such a statement is contained in the next result, originally due to Hukuhara and Turrittin, with generalizations and further developments concerning nonlinear equations due to Ramis and Sibuya (see Chapter 7.2 of [dPS03] for a proof and references).

Theorem 13.

Let A∈gln​(ℂ⁡({x})),A\in{\rm gl}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}(\{x\})), w∈(ℂ⁡({x}))nw\in({\mathbb{C}}(\{x\}))^{n} and v^∈(ℂ⁡((x)))n\hat{v}\in({\mathbb{C}}((x)))^{n} such that

v^′−A​v^=w.\hat{v}^{\prime}-A\hat{v}=w\ .

For any direction θ∈S1\theta\in S^{1} there exist a,b,a<θ<ba,b,\ a<\theta<b and v∈(𝒜⁡(a,b))nv\in({\mathcal{A}}(a,b))^{n} such that J⁡(v)=v^J(v)=\hat{v} and

v′−A​v=wv^{\prime}-Av=w

In general, there may be many functions vv satisfying the conclusion of the theorem. To guarantee uniqueness we will refine the notion of asymptotic expansion and require that this be valid on large enough sectors. The refined notion of asymptotics is given by

Definition 14

(1) Let kk be a positive real number, 𝒮{\mathcal{S}} an open sector. A function f∈𝒜⁡(𝒮)f\in{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{S}}) with J⁡(f)=∑n≥n0cn​xnJ(f)=\sum_{n\geq n_{0}}c_{n}x^{n} is Gevrey of order kk if for all closed W⊂𝒮,∃A>0,c>0W\subset{\mathcal{S}},\ \exists A>0,c>0 such that ∀N≥1,x∈W,|x|≤c\forall N\geq 1,\ x\in W,\ |x|\leq c one has

|f⁡(z)−∑n0≤n≤N−1cn​xn|≤AN​(N!)1k​|x|N|f(z)-\sum_{n_{0}\leq n\leq N-1}c_{n}x^{n}|\leq A^{N}(N!)^{\frac{1}{k}}|x|^{N}

(One usually uses Γ⁡(1+Nk)\Gamma(1+\frac{N}{k}) instead of (N!)1k(N!)^{\frac{1}{k}} but this makes no difference.)
(2) We denote by 𝒜1k​(𝒮){\mathcal{A}}_{\frac{1}{k}}({\mathcal{S}}) the ring of all Gevrey functions of order kk on 𝒮{\mathcal{S}} and let 𝒜1k0​(𝒮){\mathcal{A}}_{\frac{1}{k}}^{0}({\mathcal{S}}) = {f∈𝒜1k​(𝒮)|J⁡(f)=0}\{f\in{\mathcal{A}}_{\frac{1}{k}}({\mathcal{S}})\ |\ J(f)=0\}

The following is a useful criterion to determine if a function is in 𝒜1k0​(𝒮){\mathcal{A}}_{\frac{1}{k}}^{0}({\mathcal{S}}).

Lemma 15.

f∈𝒜1k0​(𝒮)f\in{\mathcal{A}}_{\frac{1}{k}}^{0}({\mathcal{S}}) if and only if ∀ closed ​W⊂𝒮,∃A,B>0\forall\mbox{ closed }W\subset{\mathcal{S}},\exists\ A,B>0 such that

|f⁡(x)|≤A​exp⁡(−B​|x|−k)∀x∈W|f(x)|\leq A\exp{(-B|x|^{-k})}\ \ \forall x\in W
Example 16

f⁡(x)=e−1xk∈𝒜1k0​(𝒮),f(x)=e^{-\frac{1}{x^{k}}}\in{\mathcal{A}}_{\frac{1}{k}}^{0}({\mathcal{S}}), for 𝒮=𝒮⁡(−π2​k,π2​k){\mathcal{S}}={\mathcal{S}}(-\frac{\pi}{2k},\frac{\pi}{2k}) but not on a larger sector. This is a hint of what is to come.

Corresponding to the notion of a Gevrey function is the notion of a Gevrey series.

Definition 17

∑n≥n0cn​xn\sum_{n\geq n_{0}}c_{n}x^{n} is a Gevrey series of order kk if ∃A>0\exists A>0 such that ∀n>0​|cn|≤An​(n!)1k.\forall n>0\ |c_{n}|\leq A^{n}(n!)^{\frac{1}{k}}.
(2) ℂ​((x))1k{{\mathbb{C}}((x))_{\frac{1}{k}}}= Gevrey series of order kk.

Note that if k<ℓk<\ell then ℂ​((x))1ℓ⊂ℂ​((x))1k{\mathbb{C}}((x))_{\frac{1}{\ell}}\subset{\mathbb{C}}((x))_{\frac{1}{k}}. Using these definitions one can prove the following key facts:

  • •

    (Improved Borel-Ritt) If |b−a|<πk|b-a|<\frac{\pi}{k}, the map J:𝒜1k​(a,b)→ℂ​((x))1kJ:{\mathcal{A}}_{\frac{1}{k}}(a,b)\rightarrow{\mathbb{C}}((x))_{\frac{1}{k}} is surjective but not injective.

  • •

    (Watson’s Lemma) If |b−a|>πk|b-a|>\frac{\pi}{k}, the map J:𝒜1k​(a,b)→ℂ​((x))1kJ:{\mathcal{A}}_{\frac{1}{k}}(a,b)\rightarrow{\mathbb{C}}((x))_{\frac{1}{k}} is injective but not surjective.

Watson’s lemma motivates the next definition.

Definition 18

(1) y^∈ℂ⁡((x))\hat{y}\in{\mathbb{C}}((x)) is kk-summable in the direction d∈S1d\in S^{1} if there exists an f∈𝒜1k​(d−α2,d+α2)f\in{\mathcal{A}}_{\frac{1}{k}}(d-\frac{\alpha}{2},d+\frac{\alpha}{2}) with J⁡(f)=y^,α>π2J(f)=\hat{y},\ \alpha>\frac{\pi}{2}.
(2) y^∈ℂ⁡((x))\hat{y}\in{\mathbb{C}}((x)) is kk-summable if it is kk-summable in all but a finite number of directions

A kk-summable function has unique analytic “lifts” in many large sectors (certainly enough to cover a deleted neighborhood of the origin). I would like to say that the entries of the matrix ϕ^​(x)\hat{\phi}(x) appearing in the formal solution of a linear differential equation are kk-summable for some kk but regretably this is not exactly true and the situation is more complicated (each is a sum of kik_{i}-summable functions for possible several kik_{i}). Before I describe what does happen, it is useful to have criteria for deciding if a series y^∈ℂ⁡((x))\hat{y}\in{\mathbb{C}}((x)) is kk-summable. Such criteria can be given in terms of Borel and Laplace transforms.

Definition 19

The Formal Borel Transform ℬk{\mathcal{B}}_{k} of order kk:

ℬk:ℂ⁡[[x]]→ℂ⁡[[ζ]]{\mathcal{B}}_{k}:{\mathbb{C}}[[x]]\rightarrow{\mathbb{C}}[[\zeta]]
ℬk​(∑cn​xn)=∑cnΓ⁡(1+nk)​ζn{\mathcal{B}}_{k}(\sum c_{n}x^{n})=\sum\frac{c_{n}}{\Gamma(1+\frac{n}{k})}\zeta^{n}

Note: If y^=∑cn​xn∈ℂ​((x))1k⇒ℬ⁡(y^)\hat{y}=\sum c_{n}x^{n}\in{\mathbb{C}}((x))_{\frac{1}{k}}\Rightarrow{\mathcal{B}}(\hat{y}) has a nonzero radius of convergence.

ℬ1​(∑(−1)n​n!​xn+1)=∑(−1)n​ζn+1n+1=log⁡(1+ζ){\mathcal{B}}_{1}(\sum(-1)^{n}n!x^{n+1})=\sum(-1)^{n}\frac{\zeta^{n+1}}{n+1}=\log(1+\zeta)

The Laplace Transform ℒk,d{\mathcal{L}}_{k,d} of order kk in the direction dd: Let ff satisfy |f⁡(ζ)|≤A​exp⁡(B​|ζ|k)|f(\zeta)|\leq A\exp({B|\zeta|^{k}}) along the ray rdr_{d} from 00 to ∞\infty in direction dd. Then

ℒk,d​f​(x)=∫rdf⁡(ζ)​exp⁡(−(ζx)k)​d​((ζx)k){\mathcal{L}}_{k,d}f(x)=\int_{r_{d}}f(\zeta)\exp(-(\frac{\zeta}{x})^{k})d((\frac{\zeta}{x})^{k})

Example 22

For any ray rdr_{d} not equal to the negative real axis, the function f⁡(ζ)=log⁡(1+ζ)f(\zeta)=\log(1+\zeta) has an analytic continuation along rdr_{d}. Furthermore, for such a ray, we have

ℒ1,d​(log⁡(1+ζ))​(x)=∫dlog⁡(1+ζ)​e−ζx​d​(ζx)=∫d11+ζ​e−ζx​𝑑ζ{\mathcal{L}}_{1,d}(\log(1+\zeta))(x)=\int_{d}\log(1+\zeta)e^{-\frac{\zeta}{x}}d(\frac{\zeta}{x})=\int_{d}\frac{1}{1+\zeta}e^{-\frac{\zeta}{x}}d\zeta

Note that there are several slightly different definitions of the Borel and Laplace transforms scattered in the literature but for our purposes these difference do not affect the final results. I am following the definitions in [Bal94] and [dPS03]. The following gives useful criteria for a Gevrey series of order kk to be kk-summable (Chapter 3.1 of [Bal94] or Chapter 7.6 of [dPS03]).

Proposition 23.

y^∈ℂ​[[x]]1k\hat{y}\in{\mathbb{C}}[[x]]_{\frac{1}{k}} is kk-summable in direction dd

In this case, f=ℒk,d​(h)f={\mathcal{L}}_{k,d}(h) is its kk-sum.

Example 24

Consider y^=∑(−1)n​n!​xn+1\hat{y}=\sum(-1)^{n}n!x^{n+1}, a power series of Gevrey order 1 that is also a solution of the Euler equation. We have seen that f⁡(ζ)=ℬ1​(y^)=∑(−1)n​ζn+1n+1=log⁡(1+ζ)​ for ​|ζ|<1f(\zeta)={\mathcal{B}}_{1}(\hat{y})=\sum(-1)^{n}\frac{\zeta^{n+1}}{n+1}=\log(1+\zeta)\mbox{ for }|\zeta|<1. As we have noted in Example 22, this function can be continued outside the unit disk in any direction other than along the negative real axis. On any ray except this one, it has exponential growth of order at most 1 and its Laplace transform is

yd​(x)=ℒ1,d​(log⁡(1+ζ))​(x)=∫dlog⁡(1+ζ)​e−ζx​d​(ζx)=∫d11+ζ​e−ζx​𝑑ζ.y_{d}(x)={\mathcal{L}}_{1,d}(\log(1+\zeta))(x)=\int_{d}\log(1+\zeta)e^{-\frac{\zeta}{x}}d(\frac{\zeta}{x})=\int_{d}\frac{1}{1+\zeta}e^{-\frac{\zeta}{x}}d\zeta.

We note that this function again satisfies the Euler equation. To see this note that y⁡(x)=C​e1xy(x)=Ce^{\frac{1}{x}} is a solution of x2​y′+y=0x^{2}y^{\prime}+y=0 and so variation of constants gives us that f⁡(x)=∫0xe1x−1t​d​ttf(x)=\int_{0}^{x}e^{\frac{1}{x}-\frac{1}{t}}\frac{dt}{t} is a solution of x2​y′+y=xx^{2}y^{\prime}+y=x. for convenience let d=0d=0 and define a new variable ζ\zeta by ζx=1t−1x\frac{\zeta}{x}=\frac{1}{t}-\frac{1}{x} gives f⁡(x)=∫d=011+ζ​e−ζx​𝑑ζf(x)=\int_{d=0}\frac{1}{1+\zeta}e^{-\frac{\zeta}{x}}d\zeta. Therefore, for any ray except the negative real axis, we are able to canonically associate a function, analytic in a large sector around this ray, with the divergent series ∑(−1)n​n!​xn+1\sum(-1)^{n}n!x^{n+1} and so this series is 11-summable. Furthermore these functions will again satisfy the Euler equation. This is again a hint for what is to come.

Linear Differential Equations and Summability. It has been known since the early 20t​h20^{th} Century that a formal series solution of an analytic differential equation F⁡(x,y,y′,…,y(n))=0F(x,y,y^{\prime},\ldots,y^{(n)})=0 must Gevrey of order kk for some kk ([Mai03]). Regretably, even for linear equations, these formal solutions need not be kk summable (see [LR95]). Nonetheless, if y^\hat{y} is a vector of formal series that satisfy a linear differential equation it can be written as a sum y^=y1^+…+yt^\hat{y}=\hat{y_{1}}+\ldots+\hat{y_{t}} where each yi^\hat{y_{i}} is kik_{i} summable for some kik_{i}. This result is the culmination of the work of several authors including Ramis, Malgrange, Martinet, Sibuya and Écale (see [LR95], [Ram93] and Chapter 7.8 of [dPS03]). The kik_{i} that occur as well as the directions along which the yi^\hat{y_{i}} are not summable can be seen from the normal form of the differential equation. We need the following definitions. Let Y′=A​Y,A∈gln​(ℂ⁡({x}))Y^{\prime}=AY,\ A\in{\rm gl}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}(\{x\})) and let Y^=ϕ^​(x)​xL​eQ⁡(1/t)\hat{Y}=\hat{\phi}(x)x^{L}e^{Q(1/t)} be a formal solution with tν=xt^{\nu}=x and Q=diag⁡(q1,…,qn),qi∈1t​ℂ​[1t]Q={\rm diag}(q_{1},\ldots,q_{n}),q_{i}\in\frac{1}{t}{\mathbb{C}}[\frac{1}{t}].

Definition 25

(1) The rational number ki=1ν​(the degree of ​qi​ in ​1t)k_{i}=\frac{1}{\nu}(\mbox{the degree of }q_{i}\mbox{ in }\frac{1}{t}) is called a slope of Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY.
(2) A Stokes direction dd for a qi=c​x−ki+…q_{i}=cx^{-k_{i}}+\ldots is a direction such that R​e​(c​x−ki)=0Re(cx^{-k_{i}})=0, i.e., where eqie^{q_{i}} changes behavior.
(3) Let d1,d2d_{1},d_{2} be consecutive Stokes directions. We say that (d1,d2)(d_{1},d_{2}) is a negative Stokes pair if R​e​(c​x−ki)<0Re(cx^{-k_{i}})<0 for arg⁡(x)∈(d1,d2)\arg(x)\in(d_{1},d_{2}).
(4) A singular direction is the bisector of a negative Stokes pair.

Example 26

For the Euler equation we have that ν=1\nu=1 and Q⁡(x)=d​i​a​g​(1x,0)Q(x)=diag(\frac{1}{x},0). Therefore the slopes are {0,1}\{0,1\}. The Stokes directions are {π2,3​π2}\{\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{2}\}. The pair (π2,3​π2)(\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{2}) is a negative Stokes pair and so π\pi is the only singular direction.

With these definitions we can state

Theorem 27.

(Multisummation Theorem) Let 1/2<k1<…<kr1/2<k_{1}<\ldots<k_{r} be the slopes of Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY and let Y^∈(ℂ⁡((x)))n\hat{Y}\in({\mathbb{C}}((x)))^{n} satisfy this differential equation. For all directions dd that are not singular directions, there exist Y^i∈ℂ⁡((x))\hat{Y}_{i}\in{\mathbb{C}}((x)) such that Y^=Y^1+…+Y^r\hat{Y}=\hat{Y}_{1}+\ldots+\hat{Y}_{r}, each Y^i\hat{Y}_{i} is kik_{i}-summable in direction dd and, for yiy_{i}= the kik_{i}-sum of Y^i\hat{Y}_{i}, yd=y1+…+yry_{d}=y_{1}+\ldots+y_{r} satisfies y′=A​yy^{\prime}=Ay.

The condition that 1/2<k11/2<k_{1} is a needed technical assumption but, after a suitable change of coordinates, one can always reduce to this case. We shall refer to the element ydy_{d} as above as the multisum of Y^\hat{Y} in the direction dd.

Stokes Matrices and the Convergent Differential Galois Group. We are now in a position to describe the analytic elements which, together with the formal Galois group determine the analytic Galois group. Once again, let us assume that we have a differential equation Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY with A∈gln​(ℂ⁡({x}))A\in{\rm gl}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}(\{x\})) and assume this has a formal solution Y^=ϕ^​(x)​xL​eQ⁡(1/t)\hat{Y}=\hat{\phi}(x)x^{L}e^{Q(1/t)} with ϕ^​(x)∈GLn​(ℂ⁡((x)))\hat{\phi}(x)\in{\rm GL}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}((x))). The matrix F=ϕ^​(x)F=\hat{\phi}(x) is a formal solution of the n2×n2n^{2}\times n^{2} system

d​Fd​x=A​F−F​A0\displaystyle\frac{dF}{dx}=AF-FA_{0} (3)

where Y′=A0​YY^{\prime}=A_{0}Y is the normal form of Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY. We will want to associate functions, analytic in sectors, to ϕ^​(x)\hat{\phi}(x) and therefore will apply the Multisummation Theorem to equation 3 (and not to Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY). One can show that the eigenvalues of equation (3) are of the form qi−qjq_{i}-q_{j} where the qi,qjq_{i},q_{j} are eigenvalues of Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY.

Let dd be a singular direction of Y′=A​Y−Y​A0Y^{\prime}=AY-YA_{0}. Select d+d^{+} and d−d^{-} nearby so that the associated sectors overlap and contain dd. Let ϕ+,ϕ−\phi^{+},\phi^{-} be the associated multisums. We must have ϕ+​xL​eQ⁡(1/t)=ϕ−​xL​eQ⁡(1/t)⋅S​td\phi^{+}x^{L}e^{Q(1/t)}=\phi^{-}x^{L}e^{Q(1/t)}\cdot St_{d} for some S​td∈GLn​(ℂ)St_{d}\in{\rm GL}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) on the overlap of the regions (the shaded area in the figure). The matrix S​tdSt_{d} is independent of the choice of d+d^{+} and d−d^{-}.

Definition 28

The matrix S​tdSt_{d} is called a Stokes matrix in the direction dd.

    Singular direction of Y′=A​Y−Y​A0Y^{\prime}=AY-YA_{0}: d=πd=\pi

    ϕ^​(x)=(1f^−1x2f^′)f^=∑n=0∞(−1)n​xn+1\hat{\phi}(x)=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}1&\hat{f}\\ -\frac{1}{x^{2}}&\hat{f}^{\prime}\end{array}\right)\ \ \ \hat{f}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{n}x^{n+1}

For d+d+ and d−d^{-} close to the negative real axis, we have

f+=∫d+11+ζ​e−ζx​𝑑ζ​ and ​f−=∫d−11+ζ​e−ζx​𝑑ζ.f^{+}=\int_{d^{+}}\frac{1}{1+\zeta}e^{-\frac{\zeta}{x}}d\zeta\mbox{ and }f^{-}=\int_{d^{-}}\frac{1}{1+\zeta}e^{-\frac{\zeta}{x}}d\zeta.

Since f+−f−=2​π​i​ Resζ=−1​(e−ζx1+ζ)=2​π​if^{+}-f^{-}=2\pi i\mbox{ Res}_{\zeta=-1}\left(\frac{e^{-\frac{\zeta}{x}}}{1+\zeta}\right)=2\pi i, we have

so S​tπ=(12​π​i01)St_{\pi}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}1&2\pi i\\ 0&1\end{array}\right)

The following result is due to Ramis [Ram85a, Ram85c, Ram85b, MR89]. Another proof appears in the work of Loday-Richaud [LR94]. An exposition of this result and its proof appears in Chapter 8 of [dPS03].

Theorem 30.

The convergent differential Galois group DGal⁡(K/ℂ⁡({x})){\rm DGal}(K/{\mathbb{C}}(\{x\})) is the Zariski closure of the group generated by

  1. 1.

    the formal differential Galois group DGal⁡(K/ℂ⁡((x))){\rm DGal}(K/{\mathbb{C}}((x))), and

    The collection of Stokes matrices {S​td}\{St_{d}\} where dd runs over the set of singular directions of the polynomials {qi−qj}\{q_{i}-q_{j}\}, qi,qjq_{i},q_{j} eigenvalues of Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY.
