We highly recommend the book [Ram93] of Ramis, the papers of Loday-Richaud [LR90, LR95] and the papers of Varadarajan [Var91, Var96] for further introductions to this analytic aspect of linear differential equations. One can find references to the original papers in these works as well as in [dPS03].

5 Algorithms

In this section we shall consider the question: Can we compute differential Galois groups and their properties? We shall not give a complete algorithm to determine the Galois groups although one exists - see [Hru02]. This general algorithm has not been implemented at present and, in its present form seems not very efficient. We will rather give a flavor of the various techniques that are presently implemented and used.
Categories motivate algorithms. We will show how results in a categorical setting concerning representations of groups lead to algorithms to determine Galois groups. We begin with an example from the Galois theory of polynomials.

Example 1

Let

P⁡(Y)=Y3+b​Y+c=0∈ℚ⁡[Y].P(Y)=Y^{3}+bY+c=0\in{\mathbb{Q}}[Y].

The usual Galois group GG of this equation is a subgroup of the full permutation group 𝒮3{\mathcal{S}}_{3} on 3 elements. We will describe how to compute GG. If P⁡(Y)=(Y+α)​(Y2+β​Y+γ),α,β,γ∈ℚP(Y)=(Y+\alpha)(Y^{2}+\beta Y+\gamma),\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in{\mathbb{Q}}, then GG is the Galois group of Y2+β​Y+γY^{2}+\beta Y+\gamma, which we assume we know how to compute. Therefore we will assume that P⁡(Y)P(Y) is irreducible over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}. This implies that GG acts transitively on the roots {ρ1,ρ2,ρ3}\{\rho_{1},\rho_{2},\rho_{3}\} of PP. From group theory we know that the only transitive subgroups of 𝒮3{\mathcal{S}}_{3} are 𝒜3{\mathcal{A}}_{3}, the alternating group on 3 elements, and 𝒮3{\mathcal{S}}_{3}. To decide which we have, consider the following associated polynomial

Z2+4​b3+27​c2=(Z+δ)​(Z−δ)δ=(r1−r2)​(r2−r3)​(r3−r1).Z^{2}+4b^{3}+27c^{2}=(Z+\delta)(Z-\delta)\ \ \delta=(r_{1}-r_{2})(r_{2}-r_{3})(r_{3}-r_{1}).

One then has that G=𝒜3G={\mathcal{A}}_{3} if Z2+4​b3+27​c2Z^{2}+4b^{3}+27c^{2} factors over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}} and G=𝒮3G={\mathcal{S}}_{3} if Z2+4​b3+27​c2Z^{2}+4b^{3}+27c^{2} irreducible over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}.

In the above example we determined the Galois group by considering factorization properties of the polynomial and associated polynomials. Why does this work?
To answer this question, let us consider a square-free polynomial f⁡(Y)∈ℚ⁡[Y]f(Y)\in{\mathbb{Q}}[Y] with roots r1,…​rn∈ℚ¯r_{1},\ldots r_{n}\in\bar{{\mathbb{Q}}}, the algebraic closure of QQ. Let GG be the Galois group of ff over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}. The group GG acts as a group of permutations on the set S={r1,…,rn}S=\{r_{1},\ldots,r_{n}\}. We have that GG acts transitively on SS if and only if the polynomial ff is irreducible. More generally, GG leaves a subset {ri1,…,rit}\{r_{i_{1}},\ldots,r_{i_{t}}\} invariant if and only if the polynomial g⁡(Y)=∏j=1t(Y−rij)∈ℚ⁡[Y]g(Y)=\prod_{j=1}^{t}(Y-r_{i_{j}})\in{\mathbb{Q}}[Y]. Therefore the orbits of GG in the set SS correspond to irreducible factors of ff. In fact, for any h∈ℚ⁡[Y]h\in{\mathbb{Q}}[Y] having all its roots in the splitting field of ff, GG-orbits in the set of roots correspond to irreducible factors of hh. In the above example, we were able to distinguish between groups because they have different orbits in certain “well-selected” sets and we were able to see this phenomenon via factorization properties of associated polynomials. The key is that, in general,

  • one can distinguish between finite groups by looking at the sets on which they act.

This strange looking statement can be formalized in the following way (see Appendix B1 of [dPS03] for details). For any finite set, let Perm⁡(S){\rm Perm}(S) be the group of permutations of SS. One constructs a category PermG{\rm Perm}_{G} of GG-sets whose objects are pairs (S,ρ)(S,\rho), where ρ:G→Perm⁡(S)\rho:G\rightarrow{\rm Perm}(S) is the map defining an action of GG on SS. The morphisms of this category are just maps between GG-sets that commute with the action of GG. One has the forgetful functor ω:PermG→Sets\omega:{\rm Perm}_{G}\rightarrow{\rm Sets} which takes (S,ρ)(S,\rho) to SS. One then has the formalization of the above statement as: one can recover the group from the pair (PermG,ω)({\rm Perm}_{G},\omega). A consequence of this is that given two groups H⊂GH\subset G there is a set SS on which GG (and therefore HH) acts so that the orbit structures with respect to these two groups are different.
These facts lead to the following strategy to compute Galois groups of a polynomial f∈ℚ⁡[X]f\in{\mathbb{Q}}[X]. For each pair of groups H⊂G⊂𝒮nH\subset G\subset{\mathcal{S}}_{n} we construct a polynomial fH,G∈ℚ⁡[X]f_{H,G}\in{\mathbb{Q}}[X] whose roots can be expressed in terms of the roots of ff and such that HH and GG can be distinguished by their orbit structures on the roots of fH,Gf_{H,G} (by the above facts, we know that there is a set that distinguishes HH from GG and one can show that this set can be constructed from the roots of ff). The factorization properties of fH,Gf_{H,G} will then distinguish HH from GG. This is what was done in Example 1.
To generalize the above ideas to calculating differential Galois groups of linear differential equations, we must first see what determines a linear algebraic group. In fact, just as finite groups are determined by their permutation representations, linear algebraic groups are determined by their linear representations. To make this more precise, let GG be a linear group algebraic group defined over an algebraically closed field CC. I will denote by RepG{\rm Rep}_{G} the category of linear representations of GG. The objects of this category are pairs (V,ρ)(V,\rho) where VV is a finite dimensional vector space over CC and ρ:G→GLn​(V)\rho:G\rightarrow{\rm GL}_{n}(V) is a representation of GG. The morphisms m:(V1,ρ1)→(V2,ρ2)m:(V_{1},\rho_{1})\rightarrow(V_{2},\rho_{2}) are linear maps m:V1→V2m:V_{1}\rightarrow V_{2} such that m∘ρ1=ρ2∘mm\circ\rho_{1}=\rho_{2}\circ m. One can define subobjects, quotients, duals, direct sums and tensor products in obvious ways (see Appendix B2 and B3 of [dPS03] for details). One again has a forgetful functor ω:RepG→VectC\omega:{\rm Rep}_{G}\rightarrow{\rm Vect}_{C} (where VectC{\rm Vect}_{C} is the category of vector spaces over CC) given by ω⁡(V,ρ)=V\omega(V,\rho)=V. In analogy to the finite group case, we have Tannaka’s Theorem, that says that we can recover GG from the pair (RepG,ω)({\rm Rep}_{G},\omega).
Let 𝒯{\mathcal{T}} be a category with a notion of quotients, duals, direct sums, tensor products and a functor ω~:𝒯→VectC\tilde{\omega}:{\mathcal{T}}\rightarrow{\rm Vect}_{C}. An example of such a category is the category of differential modules 𝒟{\mathcal{D}} over a differential field kk with algebraically closed constants and ω~(M)=ker(∂,K⊗M)\tilde{\omega}(M)=\ker({\partial},K\otimes M) (see the discussion following Definition 13) where KK is a differential field large enough to contain solutions of the differential equations corresponding to the modules in 𝒟{\mathcal{D}}. One can give axioms that guarantee that ω~​(𝒯)\tilde{\omega}({\mathcal{T}}) “=” ω⁡(RepG)\omega({\rm Rep}_{G}) for some linear algebraic group GG (see [DM82], [Del90] or Appendix B3 of [dPS03]). Such a pair (𝒯,ω~)({\mathcal{T}},\tilde{\omega}) is called a neutral tannakian category. Applying this to a subcategory of 𝒟{\mathcal{D}}, one has:

Theorem 2.

Let (k,∂)(k,{\partial}) be a differential field with algebraically closed constants, let Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY be a linear differential equation over (k,∂)(k,{\partial}), let MAM_{A} be the associated differential module and KK the associated Picard-Vessiot extension. Let 𝒯={{MA}}{\mathcal{T}}=\{\{M_{A}\}\} be the smallest subcategory of 𝒟{\mathcal{D}} containing MAM_{A} and closed under the operations of taking submodules, quotients, duals, direct sums , and tensor products. For N∈{{MA}}N\in\{\{M_{A}\}\}, let ω~(N)=ker(∂,N⊗K)\tilde{\omega}(N)=\ker({\partial},N\otimes K).
Then (𝒯,ω~)({\mathcal{T}},\tilde{\omega}) is a neutral tannakian category and the image of ω~\tilde{\omega} is the category of vector spaces on which DGal⁡(K/k){\rm DGal}(K/k) acts.

This theorem and Tannaka’s Theorem have the following implications:

  • •

    One can construct all representations of DGal⁡(K/k){\rm DGal}(K/k) by:

    • –

      using the constructions of linear algebra (submodules, quotients, duals, direct sums, tensor products) on MAM_{A}, and

    • –

      taking the solution spaces of the corresponding differential equations.

  • •

    DGal⁡(K/k){\rm DGal}(K/k) is determined by knowing which subspaces of these solution spaces are DGal⁡(K/k){\rm DGal}(K/k)-invariant.

At first glance, it seems that one would need to consider an infinite number of differential modules but in many cases, it is enough to consider only a finite number of modules constructed from MAM_{A}. Regretably, there are groups (for example, any group of the form C∗⊕…⊕C∗C^{*}\oplus\ldots\oplus C^{*}) for which on needs an infinite number of representations to distinguish it from other groups. Nonetheless, there are many groups where a finite number of representations suffice. Furthermore, Proposition 28 states that the DGal{\rm DGal}-invariant subspaces of the solution space of a differential module NN correspond to factors of the associated scalar equation LN​(Y)=0L_{N}(Y)=0. Therefore, in many cases, one can give criteria for a differential equation to have a given group as Galois group in terms of factorization properties of certain associated differential operators. We shall give examples for second order equations. We begin with a definition.
Let kk be a differential field with algebraically closed constants CC, let L=∂2−s∈k[∂]L={\partial}^{2}-s\in k[{\partial}], and let KK be the Picard-Vessiot extension corresponding to L⁡(Y)=0L(Y)=0. Let {y1,y2}\{y_{1},y_{2}\} be a basis for the solution space VV of L⁡(Y)=0L(Y)=0 in KK and let Vm=C−span of ​{y1m,y1m−1​y2,…,y2m}V_{m}=C-\mbox{span of }\{y_{1}^{m},y_{1}^{m-1}y_{2},\ldots,y_{2}^{m}\}. One can see that VmV_{m} is independent of the selected basis of VV and that it is invariant under the action of DGal⁡(K/k){\rm DGal}(K/k). As in the proof of Proposition 28 one can show that this implies that VmV_{m} is precisely the solution space of a scalar linear differential equation over kk.

To see this it is enough to show that the y1m−i​y2i, 0≤i≤my_{1}^{m-i}y_{2}^{i},\ 0\leq i\leq m are linearly independent over CC. m=2m=2:

The vector spaces VmV_{m} correspond to representations of DGal⁡(K/k){\rm DGal}(K/k) on the mt​hm^{th} symmetric power of VV and are well understood for many groups [FH91] (the mt​hm^{th} symmetric power of a vector space is the vector space with a basis formed by the monomials of degree mm in a basis of VV). Using representation theory, one can show:

Proposition 5.

Let L⁡(y)=y′′−s​yL(y)=y^{\prime\prime}-sy and let G=DGal⁡(K/k)G={\rm DGal}(K/k). Assume LL and L○s​2L^{{\scriptstyle\bigcirc\hskip-6.544pt\raisebox{0.5123pt}{${\scriptstyle s}$}}\hskip 2.84544pt2} are irreducible.

    If L○s​3L^{{\scriptstyle\bigcirc\hskip-6.544pt\raisebox{0.5123pt}{${\scriptstyle s}$}}\hskip 2.84544pt3} is reducible. then G/±I≃A4\ G/\pm I\simeq A_{4}.

    If L○s​3L^{{\scriptstyle\bigcirc\hskip-6.544pt\raisebox{0.5123pt}{${\scriptstyle s}$}}\hskip 2.84544pt3} is reducible and L○s​4L^{{\scriptstyle\bigcirc\hskip-6.544pt\raisebox{0.5123pt}{${\scriptstyle s}$}}\hskip 2.84544pt4} is irreducible then G/±I≃S4\ G/\pm I\simeq S_{4}.

    If L○s​6L^{{\scriptstyle\bigcirc\hskip-6.544pt\raisebox{0.5123pt}{${\scriptstyle s}$}}\hskip 2.84544pt6}is irreducible then G≃SL2​(C)\ G\simeq{\rm SL}_{2}(C).

In order to implement these criteria, one needs good algorithms to factor linear operators. Such algorithms exist and I refer to Chapter 4.2 of [dPS03] for descriptions of some algorithms that factor linear operators as well as further references to the extensive literature. The calculation of symmetric powers and factorization of operators has been implemented in Maple in the DEtools package.
One can develop similar criteria for higher order operators. Given a differential operator LL of order nn with {y1,…,yn}\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}\} being a basis of the solution space VV in some Picard-Vessiot extension, one can consider the CC-space VmV_{m} of homogeneous polynomials of degree mm in the yiy_{i}. This space has dimension at most (m+n−1n−1)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}m+n-1\\ n-1\end{array}\right) but may have dimension that is strictly smaller and so is not isomorphic to the mt​hm^{th} symmetric power of VV (although it is isomorphic to a quotient). This complicates matters but this situation can be dealt with by casting things directly in terms of differential modules, forming the symmetric powers of differential modules and developing algorithms to find submodules of differential modules. This is explained in Chapter 4.2 of [dPS03]. Examples of criteria for third order equations are given in Chapter 4.3.5 of [dPS03] where further references are given as well.
Solving L⁡(y)=0L(y)=0 in terms of exponentials, integrals and
algebraics. I shall give a formal definition that captures the meaning of this term.

Definition 6

Let kk be a differential field, L∈k[∂]L\in k[{\partial}], and KK be the associated Picard-Vessiot extension.
1) A liouvillian tower over kk is a tower of differential fields k=K0⊂…⊂Kmk=K_{0}\subset\ldots\subset K_{m} with K⊂KmK\subset K_{m} and, for each i,0≤i<mi,0\leq i<m, Ki+1=Ki​(ti)K_{i+1}=K_{i}(t_{i}), with

  • •

    tit_{i} algebraic over KiK_{i}, or

  • •

    ti′∈Kit_{i}^{\prime}\in K_{i}, i.e., ti=∫ui,ui∈Kit_{i}=\int u_{i},u_{i}\in K_{i}, or

  • •

    ti′/ti∈Kit_{i}^{\prime}/t_{i}\in K_{i}, i.e., ti=e∫ui,ui∈Kit_{i}=e^{\int u_{i}},u_{i}\in K_{i}

2) An element of liouvillian tower is said to be liouvillian over k.
3) L⁡(y)=0L(y)=0 is solvable in terms of liouvillian functions if the associated PV-extension KK lies in a liouvillian tower over kk.

Picard and Vessiot stated the following Galois theoretic criteria and this was given a formal modern proof by Kolchin [Kol48, Kol76].

Theorem 7.

Let k,L,k,L, and KK be as above. L⁡(y)=0L(y)=0 is solvable in terms of liouvillian functions if and only if the identity component (in the Zarski topology) of DGal⁡(K/k){\rm DGal}(K/k) is solvable.

Recall that a group GG is solvable if there exists a tower of subgroups G=G0⊃G1⊃…⊃Gm={e}G=G_{0}\supset G_{1}\supset\ldots\supset G_{m}=\{e\} such that Gi+1G_{i+1} is normal in GiG_{i} and Gi+1/GiG_{i+1}/G_{i} is abelian. This above theorem depends on the

Theorem 8.

(Lie-Kolchin Theorem) Let CC be an algebraically closed field. A Zariski connected solvable group G⊂GLn​(C)G\subset{\rm GL}_{n}(C) is conjugate to a groups of triangular matrices. In particular, GG leaves a one dimensional subspace invariant.

I shall show how the Lie-Kolchin Theorem can be strengthened resulting in a strengthened version of Theorem 7 that leads to an algorithm to decide if a given linear differential equation (over C⁡(x)C(x)) can be solved in terms of liouvillian functions. I begin with

Proposition 9.

Let kk be a differential field, L∈k[∂]L\in k[{\partial}], KK the corresponding Picard-Vessiot extensions and GG the differential Galois group of KK over kk. The following are equivalent:

  1. 1.

    L⁡(y)=0L(y)=0 has a liouvillian solution ≠0\neq 0.

  2. 2.

    GG has a subgroup H,|G:H|=m<∞H,|G:H|=m<\infty such that HH leaves a one dimensional subspace invariant.

  3. 3.

    L⁡(y)=0L(y)=0 has a soln z≠0z\neq 0 such that z′/zz^{\prime}/z algebraic over kk of degree ≤m\leq m.

Proof 5.1.

(Outline; see Chapter 4.3 of [dPS03]) (iii) ⇒\Rightarrow(i): Clear.
(i) ⇒\Rightarrow(ii): One can reduce this to the case where all solutions are liouvillian. In this case, the Lie-Kolchin Theorem implies that the identity component G0G^{0} of GG leaves a one dimensional subspace invariant.
(ii) ⇒\Rightarrow(iii): Let V=S​o​l​n​(L)V=Soln(L) and v∈Vv\in V span an HH-invariant line. We then have that ∀σ∈H,∃cσ∈Ck\forall\sigma\in H,\exists c_{\sigma}\in C_{k} such that σ⁡(v)=cσ​v\sigma(v)=c_{\sigma}v. This implies that ∀σ∈H,σ⁡(v′v)=(c​v)′c​v=v′v\forall\sigma\in H,\sigma(\frac{v^{\prime}}{v})=\frac{(cv)^{\prime}}{cv}=\frac{v^{\prime}}{v}. Therefore, the Fundamental Theorem implies that v′v∈E=\frac{v^{\prime}}{v}\in E= fixed field of HH. One can show that [E:k]=|G:H|=m[E:k]=|G:H|=m so v′v\frac{v^{\prime}}{v} is algebraic over kk of degree at most mm.

In order to use this result, one needs a bound on the integer mm that can appear in (ii) and (iii) above. This is supplied by the following group theoretic result (see Chapter 4.3.1 of [dPS03] for references).

Lemma 10.

There exists a function I⁡(n)I(n) such that if G⊂GLn​(ℂ),H⊂GG\subset{\rm GL}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}),H\subset G satisfies

  1. 1.

    |G:H|<∞|G:H|<\infty and

  2. 2.

    HH leaves a one dimension subspace invariant

then there exists a subsgroup H~⊂G\tilde{H}\subset G such that

  1. 1.

    |G:H~|<I(n)|G:\tilde{H}|<I(n) and

  2. 2.

    H~\tilde{H} leaves a one dimensional subspace invariant.

In general we know that I⁡(n)≤n2​n2+2I(n)\leq n^{2n^{2}+2}. For small values of nn we have exact values, (e.g., I(2) = 12, I(3) = 360). This clearly allows us to deduce the following corollary to Proposition 9.

Corollary 11.

Let k,L,Kk,L,K be as in Propostion 9 with the order of LL equal to nn. The following are equivalent

  1. 1.

    L⁡(y)=0L(y)=0 has a liouvillian solution ≠0\neq 0.

  2. 2.

    GG has a subgroup H,|G:H|≤I(n)H,|G:H|\leq I(n) such that HH leaves a one dimensional subspace invariant.

  3. 3.

    L⁡(y)=0L(y)=0 has a soln z≠0z\neq 0 such that z′/zz^{\prime}/z algebraic /k/k of deg ≤I⁡(n)\leq I(n).

This last result leads to several algorithms to decide if a differential equation L⁡(y)=0L(y)=0, L∈C(x)[∂],CL\in C(x)[{\partial}],C a finitely generated subfield of ℂ{\mathbb{C}}, has a liouvillian solution. The one presented in [Sin81] (containing ideas going back to [Bou98]) searches for a putative minimal polynomial P⁡(u)=am​um+am−1​um−1+…+a0,ai∈ℂ⁡[x]P(u)=a_{m}u^{m}+a_{m-1}u^{m-1}+\ldots+a_{0},\ a_{i}\in{\mathbb{C}}[x] of an element u=z′/zu=z^{\prime}/z where zz is a solution of L⁡(y)=0L(y)=0 and m≤I⁡(n)m\leq I(n). This algorithm shows how the degrees of the aia_{i} in xx can be bounded in terms of information calculated at each singular point of LL. Once one has degree bounds, the actual coefficients aia_{i} can be shown to satisfy a system of polynomial equations and one can (in theory) use various techniques (e.g., Gröbner bases) to solve these. Many improvements and new ideas have been given since then (see Chapter 4 of [dPS03]). We shall present criteria that form the basis of one method, describe what one needs to do to use this in general and give details for finding liouvillian solutions of second order differential equations.

Proposition 12.

(1) Let GG be a subgroup of GLn{\rm GL}_{n}. There exists a subgroup H⊂G,|G:H|≤I(n)H\subset G,|G:H|\leq I(n) with HH leaving a one dimensional space invariant if and only if GG permutes a set of at most I⁡(n)I(n) one dimensional subspaces.
(2) Let k,L,K,Gk,L,K,G be as in Propostion 9 with the order of LL equal to nn. Then L⁡(y)=0L(y)=0 has a liovuillian solution if and only if G⊂GLnG\subset{\rm GL}_{n} permutes a set of at most I⁡(n)I(n) one dimensional subspaces.

Proof 5.2.

(1) Let ℓ\ell be a one dimensional space left invariant by HH. The orbit of ℓ\ell under the action of GG has dimension at most |G:H||G:H|. Now, let ℓ\ell be a one dimensional space whose orbit under GG is at most I⁡(n)I(n) and let HH be the stabiliizer of ℓ\ell. We then have |G:H|≤I(n)|G:H|\leq I(n). (2) is an immediate consequence of (1) and the previous proposition.

To apply this result, we need the following definition:

Definition 13

Let VV be a vector space of dimension nn and t≥1t\geq 1 be an integer. The tt​ht^{th} symmetric power Symt​(V){\rm Sym}^{t}(V)of VV is the quotient of the t−f​o​l​dt-fold tensor product V⊗tV^{\otimes t} by the subspace generated by elements v1⊗…⊗vt−vπ⁡(1)⊗…⊗vπ⁡(t)v_{1}\otimes\ldots\otimes v_{t}-v_{\pi(1)}\otimes\ldots\otimes v_{\pi(t)}, for all vi∈Vv_{i}\in V and π\pi a permutation.

We denote by v1v2⋯vtv_{1}v_{2}\cdots v_{t} the image of v1⊗…⊗vtv_{1}\otimes\ldots\otimes v_{t} in Symt​(V){\rm Sym}^{t}(V). If e1,…,ene_{1},\ldots,e_{n} is a basis of VV and 1≤t≤n1\leq t\leq n, then {ei1ei2⋯eit|i1<i2<…<it}\{e_{i_{1}}e_{i_{2}}\cdots e_{i_{t}}\ |\ i_{1}<i_{2}<\ldots<i_{t}\} is a basis of Symt​(V){\rm Sym}^{t}(V). Furthermore, if G⊂GLn​(V)G\subset{\rm GL}_{n}(V), then GG acts on Symt​(V){\rm Sym}^{t}(V) as well via the formula σ(v1⋯vt)=σ(v1)⋯σ(vt),σ∈G\sigma(v_{1}\cdots v_{t})=\sigma(v_{1})\cdots\sigma(v_{t}),\sigma\in G.

Definition 14

(1) An element w∈Symt​(V)w\in{\rm Sym}^{t}(V) is decomposable if w=w1⋯wtw=w_{1}\cdots w_{t} for some wi∈Vw_{i}\in V.
(2) A one dimensional subspace ℓ⊂Symt​(V)\ell\subset{\rm Sym}^{t}(V) is decomposable if ℓ\ell is spanned by a decomposable vector.

We note that if we fix a basis {e1,…,en}\{e_{1},\ldots,e_{n}\} of VV then an element

∑i1<…<itci1​…​itei1⋯eit\sum_{i_{1}<\ldots<i_{t}}c_{i_{1}\ldots i_{t}}e_{i_{1}}\cdots e_{i_{t}}

is decomposable if and only if the ci1​…​itc_{i_{1}\ldots i_{t}} satisfy a system of equations called the Brill equations ([GKZ94], p. 120,140). Using these definitions, it is not hard to show

Proposition 15.

(1) A group G⊂GLn​(V)G\subset{\rm GL}_{n}(V) permutes a set of tt one dimensional subspaces if and only if GG leaves a decomposable one dimensional subspace of Symt​(V){\rm Sym}^{t}(V) invariant.
(2) Let k,L,K,Gk,L,K,G be as in Propostion 9 with the order of LL equal to nn. Then L⁡(y)=0L(y)=0 has a liovuillian solution if and only if for some t≤I⁡(n)t\leq I(n) GG leaves invariant a one dimensional subspace of Symt​(Soln​(L)){\rm Sym}^{t}({\rm Soln}(L)).

Note that Symt​(V){\rm Sym}^{t}(V) is constructed using tensor products and quotients. When we apply this construction to differential modules, we get

Definition 16

Let kk be a differential field and MM a differential module over kk. The tt​ht^{th} symmetric power Symt​(M){\rm Sym}^{t}(M)of MM is the quotient of the tt-fold tensor product M⊗tM^{\otimes t} by the kk-subspace generated by elements v1⊗…⊗vt−vπ⁡(1)⊗…⊗vπ⁡(t)v_{1}\otimes\ldots\otimes v_{t}-v_{\pi(1)}\otimes\ldots\otimes v_{\pi(t)}, for all vi∈Vv_{i}\in V and π\pi a permutation (note that this subspace is a differential submodule as well).

At the end of Section 1.2, I defined the solution space of a kk-differential module MM in a differential field K⊃kK\supset k to be SolnK(M)=ker(∂,K⊗kM){\rm Soln}_{K}(M)=\ker({\partial},K\otimes_{k}M). From our discussion of tannakian categories, we have that SolnK​(Symt​(M))=Symt​(SolnK​(M)){\rm Soln}_{K}({\rm Sym}^{t}(M))={\rm Sym}^{t}({\rm Soln}_{K}(M)). This latter fact suggests the following algorithm to decide if a linear differential equation has a liouvillian solution (we continue to work with scalar equations although everything generalizes easily to systems). Let MLM_{L} be the differential module associated to the equation L⁡(y)=0L(y)=0. For each t≤I⁡(n)t\leq I(n)

  • •

    Calculate Nt=Symt​(M)N_{t}={\rm Sym}^{t}(M) and find all one dimensional submodules.

The tannakian formalism implies that a one dimensional submodule of NtN_{t} is decomposable if and only if its solution space is a decomposable subspace GG-invariant subspace of Symt​(SolnK​(ML)){\rm Sym}^{t}({\rm Soln}_{K}(M_{L})).
Much work has been done on developing algorithms for these two step. The problem of finding one dimensional submodules of a differential module was essentially solved in the 19t​h19^{th} and early 20t​h20^{th} Centuries (albeit in a different language). More recently work of Barkatou, Bronstein van Hoeij, Li, Weil, Wu, Zhang and others has produced good algorithms to solve this problem (see [HW96], [HRUW99], [LSWZ06] and Chapter 4.3.2 of [dPS03] for references). As noted above, the second problem can be solved (in principal) using the Brill equations (see [SU97] and Chapter 4.3.2 of [dPS03] for a fuller discussion). Finally, one can modify the above to produce the liouvillian solutions as well.
Before I explicate these ideas further in the context of second order equations, I will say a few words concerning finding invariant one dimensional subspaces of solution spaces of linear scalar equations.

Another approach to second order linear differential equations was discovered by Felix Klein. It has been put in modern terms by Dwork and Baldassari and made more effective recently by van Hoeij and Weil (see [HW05] for references).

Solving in Terms of Lower Order Equations. Another way of defining the notion of “solving in terms of liouvillian functions” is to say that a linear differential equation can be solved in terms of solutions of first order equations Y′+a​Y=bY^{\prime}+aY=b and algebraic functions. With this in mind it is natural to make the following definition.

Definition 21

Let kk be a differential field, L∈k[∂]L\in k[{\partial}] and KK the associated Picard-Vessiot extension. The equation L⁡(Y)=0L(Y)=0 is solvable in terms of lower order linear equations if there exists a tower k=K0⊂K1⊂…⊂Kmk=K_{0}\subset K_{1}\subset\ldots\subset K_{m} with K⊂KmK\subset K_{m} and for each i,0≤i<mi,0\leq i<m, Ki+1=Ki<ti>K_{i+1}=K_{i}<t_{i}> (Ki+1K_{i+1} is generated as a differential field by tit_{i} and KiK_{i}), with

  • •

    tit_{i} algebraic over KiK_{i}, or

  • •

    Li(ti)=bi for some Li∈Ki[∂]ord(Li)<ord(L),bi∈KiL_{i}(t_{i})=b_{i}\mbox{ for some }L_{i}\in K_{i}[{\partial}]\ ord(L_{i})<ord(L),\ b_{i}\in K_{i}

One has the following characterization of this property in terms of the differential Galois group.

Theorem 22.

([Sin88]) Let k,L,Kk,L,K be as above with o​r​d​(L)=n{\mathrm{o}rd}(L)=n. The equation L⁡(Y)=0L(Y)=0 is not solvable in terms of lower order linear equations if and only if the lie algebra of DGal⁡(K/k){\rm DGal}(K/k) is simple and has no faithful representations of dimension less than nn.

If o​r​d​(L)=3{\mathrm{o}rd}(L)=3, then an algorithm to determine if this equation is solvable in terms of lower order linear equations is given in [Sin85]. Refinements of this algorithm and extensions to higher order LL are given in [H02], [H07], [Ngu07], [NdP07], [Per02].

6 Inverse Problems

In this section we consider the following problem:
Given a differential field kk, characterize those linear differential algebraic groups that appear as differential Galois groups of Picard-Vessiot extensions over kk.
We begin with considering the inverse problem over fields of constants.
Differential Galois groups over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}. Let L∈ℂ[∂]L\in{\mathbb{C}}[{\partial}] be a linear differential operator with constant coefficients. All solutions of L(Y)=0,L∈ℂ[∂]L(Y)=0,\ L\in{\mathbb{C}}[{\partial}] are of the form ∑iPi​(x)​eαi​x\sum_{i}P_{i}(x)e^{\alpha_{i}x} where Pi​(x)∈ℂ​[x]P_{i}(x)\in{\mathbb{C}}[x], αi∈ℂ,x′=1\alpha_{i}\in{\mathbb{C}},x^{\prime}=1. This implies that the associated Picard-Vessiot KK is a subfield of a field E=ℂ⁡(x,eα1​x,…,eαt​x)E={\mathbb{C}}(x,e^{\alpha_{1}x},\ldots,e^{\alpha_{t}x}). One can show that DGal⁡(E/k)=(ℂ,+)×((ℂ∗,⋅)×…×(ℂ∗,⋅)){\rm DGal}(E/k)=({\mathbb{C}},+)\times(({\mathbb{C}}^{*},\cdot)\times\ldots\times({\mathbb{C}}^{*},\cdot)). The group DGal⁡(K/ℂ){\rm DGal}(K/{\mathbb{C}}) is a quotient of this latter group and one can show that it therefore must be of the form (ℂ,+)a×(ℂ∗,⋅)b,a=0,1,b∈ℕ.({\mathbb{C}},+)^{a}\times({\mathbb{C}}^{*},\cdot)^{b},a=0,1,\ b\in{\mathbb{N}}.

One can furthermore characterize in purely group theoretic term the groups that appear as differential Galois groups over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}. Note that

(ℂ,+)≃{(1a01)|a∈ℂ}({\mathbb{C}},+)\simeq\{\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}1&a\\ 0&1\end{array}\right)\ |\ a\in{\mathbb{C}}\}

and that all these elements are unipotent matrices (i.e., (A−I)m=0(A-I)^{m}=0 for some m≠0m\neq 0). This motivates the following definition

Definition 1

If GG is a linear differnetial algebraic group, the unipotent radical RuR_{u} of GG is the largest normal subgroup of GG all of whose elements are unipotent.

Note that for a group of the form G=ℂ×(ℂ∗×…×ℂ∗)G={\mathbb{C}}\times({\mathbb{C}}^{*}\times\ldots\times{\mathbb{C}}^{*}) we have that Ru​(G)=ℂR_{u}(G)={\mathbb{C}}. Using facts about linear algebraic groups (see [Hum75] or[Spr98]) one can characterize those linear algebraic groups that appear as differential Galois groups over an algebraically closed field of constants CC as

Proposition 2.

A linear algebraic group GG is a differential Galois group of a Picard-Vessiot extension of (ℂ,∂),∂c=∀c∈ℂ({\mathbb{C}},{\partial}),{\partial}c=\forall c\in{\mathbb{C}} if and only if GG is connected, abelian and Ru​(G)≤1R_{u}(G)\leq 1.

All of the above holds equally well for any algebraically closed field CC.
Differential Galois groups over ℂ⁡(x),x′=1{\mathbb{C}}(x),x^{\prime}=1. The inverse problem for this field was first solved by C. and M. Tretkoff, who showed

Theorem 3.

[TT79] Any linear algebraic group is a differential Galois group of a Picard-Vessiot extension of ℂ⁡(x){\mathbb{C}}(x).

Their proof (which I will outline below) depends on the solution of Hilbert’s 21s​t21^{st} Problem. This problem has a weak and strong form. Let 𝒮={α1,…,αm,∞}⊂S2{\mathcal{S}}=\{\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{m},\infty\}\subset S^{2}, α0∈S2−𝒮\alpha_{0}\in S^{2}-{\mathcal{S}} and ρ:π1​(S2−𝒮,α0)→GLn​(ℂ)\rho:\pi_{1}(S^{2}-{\mathcal{S}},\alpha_{0})\rightarrow{\rm GL}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) be a homomorphism.
Weak Form Does there exist A∈gln​(ℂ​(x))A\in{\rm gl}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}(x)) such that

  • •

    Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY has only regular singular points, and

  • •

    The monodromy representation of Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY is ρ\rho.

Strong Form Do there exist Ai∈GLn​(ℂ)A_{i}\in{\rm GL}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) such that the monodromy rep of

Y′=(A1x−α1+…+Amx−αm)​YY^{\prime}=(\frac{A_{1}}{x-\alpha_{1}}+\ldots+\frac{A_{m}}{x-\alpha_{m}})Y

is ρ\rho.
We know that a differential equation Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY that has a regular singular point is locally equivalent to one with a simple pole. The strong form of the problem insists that we find an equation that is globally equivalent to one with only simple poles. A solution of the strong form of the problem of course yields a solution of the weak form. Many special cases of the strong form were solved before a counterexample to the general case was found by Bolibruch (see [Bea93], [AB94] or Chapters 5 and 6 of [dPS03] for a history and exposition of results and [BMM06] for more recent work and generalizations).

  1. 1.

    Let γ1,…,γm\gamma_{1},\ldots,\gamma_{m} be generators of π1​(S2−𝒮,α0)\pi_{1}(S^{2}-{\mathcal{S}},\alpha_{0}), each enclosing just one αi\alpha_{i}. If some ρ⁡(γi)\rho(\gamma_{i}) is diagonalizable, then the answer is yes. (Plemelj)

  2. 2.

    If all ρ⁡(γi)\rho(\gamma_{i}) are sufficiently close to II, the answer is yes. (Lappo-Danilevsky)

  3. 3.

    If n=2n=2, the answer is yes. (Dekkers)

  4. 4.

    If ρ\rho is irreducible, the answer is yes. (Kostov, Bolibruch)

  5. 5.

    Counterexample for n=3,|𝒮|=4n=3,|{\mathcal{S}}|=4 and complete characterization for n=3,4n=3,4 (Bolibruch, Gladyshev)

In a sense, the positive answer to the weak from follows from Plemelj’s result above - one just needs to add an additional singular point αm+1\alpha_{m+1} and let γm+1\gamma_{m+1} be the identity matrix. A modern approach to give a positive answer to the weak form was given by Röhrl and later Deligne (see [Del70]). We now turn to
Proof of Theorem 3 (outline, see [TT79] of Chapter 5.2 or [dPS03] for details) Let GG be a linear algebraic group. One can show that there exist g1,…,gm∈Gg_{1},\ldots,g_{m}\in G that generate a Zariski dense subgroup HH. Select points 𝒮={α1,…​αm}⊂S2{\mathcal{S}}=\{\alpha_{1},\ldots\alpha_{m}\}\subset S^{2} and define ρ:π1​(S2−𝒮,α0)→H\rho:\pi_{1}(S^{2}-{\mathcal{S}},\alpha_{0})\rightarrow H via ρ⁡(γi)=gi\rho(\gamma_{i})=g_{i}. Using the solution of the weak form of Hilbert’s 21s​t21^{st}, there exist A∈gln​(ℂ​(x))A\in{\rm gl}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}(x)) such that Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY has regular singular points and monodromy gp HH. Schlesinger’s Theorem, Theorem 27, implies that the differential Galois group of this equation is the Zariski closure of HH. □\square
The above result leads to the following two questions:

  • •

    What is the minimum number of singular points (not necessarily regular singular points) that a linear differential system must have to realize a given group as its Galois group?

  • •

    Can we realize all linear algebraic group as differential Galois groups over C⁡(x),x′=1C(x),x^{\prime}=1 where CC is an arbitrary algebraically closed field?

To answer the first question, we first will consider
Differential Galois groups over ℂ⁡({x}){\mathbb{C}}(\{x\}). To characterize which groups occur as differential Galois groups over this field, we need the following definitions.

Definition 4

Let CC be an algebraically closed field.
(1) A torus is a linear algebraic group isomorphic to (C∗,⋅)r(C^{*},\cdot)^{r} for some rr.
(2) If GG is a linear algebraic group then we define L⁡(G)L(G) to be the group generated by all tori in GG. This is a normal, Zariski closed subgroup of GG (see [Ram96] and Chapter 11.3 of [dPS03]).

Examples 5

(1) If GG is reductive and connected (e.g., tori, GLn,SLn{\rm GL}_{n},{\rm SL}_{n}), then L⁡(G)=GL(G)=G (A group GG is reductive if Ru​(G)={I}R_{u}(G)=\{I\}).
(2) If G=(C,+)r,r≥2G=(C,+)^{r},r\geq 2, then L⁡(G)={I}L(G)=\{I\}.

Ramis [Ram96] showed the following (see also Chapter 11.4 of [dPS03]).

Theorem 6.

A linear algebraic group GG is a differential Galois group of a Picard-Vessiot extension of ℂ⁡({x}){\mathbb{C}}(\{x\}) if and only if G/L⁡(G)G/L(G) is the Zariski closure of a cyclic group.

Any linear algebraic group GG with G/G0G/G^{0} cyclic and GG reductive satisfies these criteria while G=(C,+)r,r≥2G=(C,+)^{r},r\geq 2 does not. Ramis showed that his characterization of local Galois groups in terms of formal monodromy, exponential torus and Stokes matrices yields a group of this type and conversely any such group can be realized as a local Galois group. Ramis was furthermore able to use analytic patching techniques to get a global version of this result.

Theorem 7.

A linear algebraic group GG is a differential Galois group of a Picard-Vessiot extension of ℂ⁡(x){\mathbb{C}}(x) with at most r−1r-1 regular singular points and one (possibly) irregular singular point if and only if G/L⁡(G)G/L(G) is the Zariski closure of a group generated by r−1r-1 elements.

Examples 8

(1) We once again have that any linear algebraic group is a differential Galois group over ℂ⁡(x){\mathbb{C}}(x) since such a group satisfies the above criteria for some rr.
(2) SLn{\rm SL}_{n} can be realized as a differential Galois group of a linear differential equation over ℂ⁡(x){\mathbb{C}}(x) with only one singular point.
(3) One needs rr singular points to realize the group (ℂ,+)r−1({\mathbb{C}},+)^{r-1} as a differential Galois group over ℂ⁡(x){\mathbb{C}}(x).

Differential Galois groups over C⁡(x)C(x), CC an algebraically closed
field. The proofs of the above results depend on analytic techniques over ℂ{\mathbb{C}} that do not necessarily apply to general algebraically closed fields CC. The paper [Sin93] examines the question of the existence of “transfer principals” and shows that for certain groups GG, the existence of an equation over ℂ⁡(x){\mathbb{C}}(x) having differential Galois group GG over implies the existence of an equation over C⁡(x)C(x) having differential Galois group GG over C⁡(x)C(x) but these results do not apply to all groups. Algebraic proofs for various groups over C⁡(x)C(x) (in fact over any differential field finitely generated over its algebraically closed field of constants) have been given over the years by Bialynicki-Birula (nilpotent groups), Kovacic (solvable groups), Mitschi/Singer(connected groups) (see [MS96] for references). Finally, Hartmann [Har05] showed that any linear algebraic group can be realized over C⁡(x)C(x) (see also [Obe03]). An exciting recent development is the announcement of a new proof by Harbater and Hartmann [Har07a, Har07c] of this fact based on a generalization of algebraic patching techniques. I will give two examples of a constructive technique (from [MS96]) that allows one to produce explicit equations for connected linear algebraic groups. This technique is based on (see Proposition 1.31 of [dPS03])

Proposition 9.

Let Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY be a differential equation over a differential field kk with algebraically closed constants CC. Let G,HG,H be linear algebraic subgroups of GLn​(C){\rm GL}_{n}(C) with lie algebras 𝒢,ℋ{\mathcal{G}},{\mathcal{H}}. Assume GG is connected.
1) Let Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY is a differential equation with A∈𝒢⊗CkA\in{\mathcal{G}}\otimes_{C}k and assume that GG is connected. Then the differential Galois group of this equation is conjugate to a subgroup of GG.
(2) Assume k=C⁡(x)k=C(x), that A∈𝒢⊗CC⁡(x)A\in{\mathcal{G}}\otimes_{C}C(x) and that the differential Galois group of Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY is H⊂GH\subset G, where HH is assumed to be connected. Then there exists B∈G⁡(C⁡(x))B\in G(C(x)) such that A~=B−1​A​B−B−1​B∈ℋ⊗CC⁡(x)\tilde{A}=B^{-1}AB-B^{-1}B\in{\mathcal{H}}\otimes_{C}C(x), that is Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY is equivalent to an equation Y′=A~​YY^{\prime}=\tilde{A}Y with A~∈𝒢⊗CC⁡(x)\tilde{A}\in{\mathcal{G}}\otimes_{C}C(x) and the equivalence is given by an element of G⁡(C⁡(x))G(C(x)).

These results allow us to formulate the following strategy to construct differential equations with differential Galois group over C⁡(x)C(x) a given connected group GG. Select A∈𝒢⊗CC⁡(x)A\in{\mathcal{G}}\otimes_{C}C(x) such that

  1. 1.

    the differential Galois group of Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY over C⁡(x)C(x) is connected, and

  2. 2.

    for any proper connected linear algebraic subgroup HH of GG, there is no B∈G⁡(C⁡(x))B\in G(C(x)) such that B−1​A​B−B−1​B∈ℋ⊗CC⁡(x)B^{-1}AB-B^{-1}B\in{\mathcal{H}}\otimes_{C}C(x).

We will assume for convenience that C⊂ℂC\subset{\mathbb{C}}. To insure that the differential Galois group is connected, we will select an element A∈𝒢⊗CC⁡[x]A\in{\mathcal{G}}\otimes_{C}C[x], that is a matrix with polynomial entries. This implies that there is a fundamental solution matrix whose entries are entire functions. Since these functions and their derivatives generate the associated Picard-Vessiot extension KK, any element of KK will be a function with at worst poles on the complex plane. If E,C⁡(x)⊂E⊂KE,C(x)\subset E\subset K is the fixed field of G0G^{0}, then the elements of EE are algebraic functions that can only be ramified at the singular points of Y′=A​YY^{\prime}=AY, that is, only at ∞\infty. But such an algebraic function must be rational so E=C⁡(x)E=C(x) and therefore G=G0G=G^{0}.
The next step is to select an A∈𝒢⊗CC⁡[x]A\in{\mathcal{G}}\otimes_{C}C[x] satisfying condition (ii) above. This is the heart of [MS96] and we shall only give two examples.

{(a00b)|a​b≠0}\{\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}a&0\\ 0&b\end{array}\right)\ |\ ab\neq 0\}

Example 11

G=SL2G={\rm SL}_{2}. Its lie algebra is sl2{\rm sl}_{2} = trace 00 matrices. Let

A=A0+x​A1=(0110)+x⁡(100−1)A=A_{0}+xA_{1}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&1\\ 1&0\end{array}\right)+x\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}1&0\\ 0&-1\end{array}\right)

It can be shown that any proper subalgebra of sl2{\rm sl}_{2} is solvable and therefore leaves a one dimensional subspace invariant. A calculation shows that no U′​U−1+U​A​U−1U^{\prime}U^{-1}+UAU^{-1} leaves a line invariant (see [MS96]) for details) and so this equation must have Galois group SL2{\rm SL}_{2}.

This latter example can be generalized to any semisimple linear algebraic group GG. Such a group can be realized as the differential Galois group of an equation of the form Y′=(A0+x​A1)​YY^{\prime}=(A_{0}+xA_{1})Y where A0A_{0} is a sum of generators of the root spaces and A1A_{1} is a sufficiently general element of the Cartan subalgebra. In general, we have

Theorem 12.

Let GG be a connected lin alg gp. defined over alg closed field CC. One can construct Ai∈gln​(C)A_{i}\in{\rm gl}_{n}(C) and A∞∈C⁡[x]A_{\infty}\in C[x] such that for distinct αi∈C\alpha_{i}\in C

Y′=(A1x−α1+…+Adx−αd+A∞)​YY^{\prime}=(\frac{A_{1}}{x-\alpha_{1}}+\ldots+\frac{A_{d}}{x-\alpha_{d}}+A_{\infty})Y

has Galois group GG.

Furthermore, the number dd in the above result coincides with the number of generators of a Zariski dense subgroup of G/L⁡(G)G/L(G) and the degree of the polynomials in A∞A_{\infty} can be bounded in terms of the groups as well. For non-connected groups [MS02] gives a construction to realize solvable-by-finite groups and [CMS05] gives a construction to realize certain semisimple-by-finite groups. Finally, many linear algebraic groups can be realized as differential Galois groups of members of classical families of differential equations [BBH88, BH89, Kat87b, Kat90, Kat96, DM89, Mit89, Mit96].
To end this section, I will mention a general inverse problem. We know that any Picard-Vessiot ring is the coordinate ring of a torsor for the differential Galois group. One can ask if every coordinate ring of a torsor for a linear algebraic group can be given the structure of a PIcard-Vessiot ring. To be more precise, let kk be a differential field withe derivation ∂{\partial} and algebraically closed constants CC. Let GG be a linear algebraic group defined over CC and VV a GG-torsor defined over kk.
Does there exist a derivation on R=k⁡[V]R=k[V] extending ∂{\partial} such that RR is a Picard-Vessiot ring with differential Galois group GG and such that the Galois action of GG on RR corresponds to the action induced by GG on the torsor VV?
When k=C⁡(x)k=C(x), this has can be answered affirmatively due to the work of [Har02]. For a general kk, finitely generated over CC, I do not know the answer. For certain groups and fields, Juan and Ledet have given positive answers, see [Jua07, JL07b, JL07a, JL07c].
Finally, the inverse problem over ℝ⁡(x){\mathbb{R}}(x) has been considered by [Dyc07].

7 Families of Linear Differential Equations

In this section we will consider a family of parameterized linear differential equations and discuss how the differential Galois group depends on the parameter. I will start by describing the situation for polynomials and the usual Galois groups. Let CC be a field and C¯\overline{C} its algebraic closure
Let G⊂𝒮mG\subset{\mathcal{S}}_{m} = fixed group of permutations and 𝒫⁡(n,m,G)={{\mathcal{P}}(n,m,G)}=

{P=∑i=0n∑j=0mai,jxiyj|ai,j∈C,Gal(P/C(x))=G}⊂C(n+1)​(m+1)\{P=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\sum_{j=0}^{m}a_{i,j}x^{i}y^{j}\ |a_{i,j}\in C,Gal(P/C(x))=G\}\subset C^{(n+1)(m+1)}

To describe the structure of 𝒫⁡(n,m,G){\mathcal{P}}(n,m,G), we need the following definition

Definition 1

A set S⊂C¯NS\subset\overline{C}^{N} is CC-constructible if it is the finite union of sets

{a∈C¯N|f1(a)=…=ft(a)=0,g(a)≠0}\{a\in\overline{C}^{N}\ |\ f_{1}(a)=\ldots=f_{t}(a)=0,g(a)\neq 0\}

where fi,g∈C⁡[X1,…,XN]f_{i},g\in C[X_{1},\ldots,X_{N}].

For example, any Zariski closed set defined over CC is CC-constructible and a subset S⊂C¯S\subset\overline{C} is C¯\overline{C}-constructible if and only if it is finite or cofinite. In particular, ℚ{\mathbb{Q}} is not ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-constructible in ℂ{\mathbb{C}}. We have the following results (see [dDR79] and the references given there)

Theorem 2.

𝒫⁡(m,n,G){\mathcal{P}}(m,n,G) is ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-constructible.

From this we can furthermore deduce

Corollary 3.

Any finite group GG is a Galois group over ℚ¯​(x)\overline{{\mathbb{Q}}}(x).

Proof 7.1.

(Outine) For G⊂𝒮mG\subset{\mathcal{S}}_{m}, one can construct an mm-sheeted normal covering of the Riemann Sphere with this as the group of deck transformations, [Tre71]. The Riemann Existence Theorem implies that this Riemann Surface is an algebraic curve and that the the Galois group of its function field over ℂ⁡(x){\mathbb{C}}(x) is GG. Therefore for some nn, 𝒫⁡(n,m,G){\mathcal{P}}(n,m,G) has a point in C(n+1)​(m+1)C^{(n+1)(m+1)}. Hilbert’s Nullstellensatz implies it will have a point in ℚ¯(n+1)​(m+1)\overline{{\mathbb{Q}}}^{(n+1)(m+1)} and therefore that GG is a Galois group over ℚ¯​(x)\overline{{\mathbb{Q}}}(x).

Differential Galois Groups of Families of Linear DifferentialEquations. I would like to apply the same strategy to linear differential equations. We begin by fixing a linear algebraic group G⊂GLmG\subset{\rm GL}_{m} and set ℒ⁡(m,n,G)={{\mathcal{L}}(m,n,G)}=

{L=∑i=0n∑j=0mai,jxi∂j|ai,j∈ℂ,Gal(L/ℂ(x))=G}⊂ℂ(n+1)​(m+1)\{L=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\sum_{j=0}^{m}a_{i,j}x^{i}{\partial}^{j}\ |a_{i,j}\in{\mathbb{C}},Gal(L/{\mathbb{C}}(x))=G\}\subset{\mathbb{C}}^{(n+1)(m+1)}

Regrettably, this set is not necessarily a ℚ{\mathbb{Q}} or even a ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-constructible set.

Example 4

We have seen that the Galois group of d​yd​x−αx​y{\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{\alpha}{x}y} is GL1​(ℂ){\rm GL}_{1}({\mathbb{C}}) if and only if α∉ℚ\alpha\notin{\mathbb{Q}}. If ℒ⁡(1,1,G​L1){\mathcal{L}}(1,1,GL_{1}) were ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-constructible then

ℒ(1,1,GL1)∩{x∂−α|α∈ℂ}=ℂ\ℚ{\mathcal{L}}(1,1,GL_{1})\cap\{x{\partial}-\alpha\ |\alpha\in{\mathbb{C}}\}={\mathbb{C}}\backslash{\mathbb{Q}}

would be constructible. Therefore, even the set ℒ⁡(1,1,G​L1){\mathcal{L}}(1,1,GL_{1}) is not ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-constructible.

Example 5

Consider the family

d2​yd​x2−(α1+α2)​d​yd​x+α1​α2​y=0G=ℂ∗⊕ℂ∗\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}-(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2})\frac{dy}{dx}+\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}y=0\hskip 21.68121ptG={\mathbb{C}}^{*}\oplus{\mathbb{C}}^{*}

If α1/α2∉ℚ​ then ​D​G​a​l=ℂ∗⊕ℂ∗\alpha_{1}/\alpha_{2}\notin{\mathbb{Q}}\mbox{ then }DGal={\mathbb{C}}^{*}\oplus{\mathbb{C}}^{*} while if α1/α2∈ℚ​ then ​D​G​a​l=ℂ∗\alpha_{1}/\alpha_{2}\in{\mathbb{Q}}\mbox{ then }DGal={\mathbb{C}}^{*}. Therefore, ℒ⁡(2,0,ℂ∗⊕ℂ∗){\mathcal{L}}(2,0,{\mathbb{C}}^{*}\oplus{\mathbb{C}}^{*}) is not ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-constructible.

Recall that for L∈ℂ(x)[∂]L\in{\mathbb{C}}(x)[{\partial}] and x0x_{0} a singular point L⁡(y)=0L(y)=0 has a fundamental set of solutions:

yi=(x−α)ρi​ePi​(1/t)​(∑j=0sibi​j​(log⁡(x−x0)j)CLOSEy_{i}=(x-\alpha)^{\rho_{i}}e^{P_{i}(1/t)}(\sum_{j=0}^{s_{i}}b_{ij}(\log(x-x_{0})^{j})

where ρi∈ℂ\rho_{i}\in{\mathbb{C}}, tℓ=(x−x0)t^{\ell}=(x-x_{0}) for some ℓ≤n!\ell\leq n!, PiP_{i} are polynomials without constant term, bi​j∈ℂ⁡[[x−x0]]b_{ij}\in{\mathbb{C}}[[x-x_{0}]].

Definition 6

The set 𝒟x0={ρ1,…,ρn,P1,…,Pn}{\mathcal{D}}_{x_{0}}=\{\rho_{1},\ldots,\rho_{n},P_{1},\ldots,P_{n}\} is called the local data of LL at x0x_{0}.

In Example 4, 00 and ∞\infty are the singular points and at both of these {α}\{\alpha\} is the local data. In Example 5, ∞\infty is the only singular point and the local data is {P1=α1x,P2=α2x}\{P_{1}=\frac{\alpha_{1}}{x},P_{2}=\frac{\alpha_{2}}{x}\}. In both cases, the parameters allow us to vary the local data. One would hope that by fixing the local data, parameterized families of linear differential equations with fixed Galois group GG would be constructible. This turns out to be true for many but not all groups GG.

Definition 7

Let 𝒟={ρ1,…,ρr,P1,…,Ps}{\mathcal{D}}=\{\rho_{1},\ldots,\rho_{r},P_{1},\ldots,P_{s}\} be a finite set with ρi∈ℂ\rho_{i}\in{\mathbb{C}} and PiP_{i} polynomials without constant terms. We define

ℒ⁡(m,n,𝒟,G)={L∈ℒ⁡(m,n,G)|𝒟a⊂𝒟​ for all sing pts ​a∈S2}{\mathcal{L}}(m,n,{\mathcal{D}},G)=\{L\in{\mathcal{L}}(m,n,G)\ |\ {\mathcal{D}}_{a}\subset{\mathcal{D}}\mbox{ for all sing pts }a\in S^{2}\}

Note that we do not fix the position of the singular points; we only fix the local data at putative singular points. Also note that ℒ(m,n,𝒟)={L=∑i=0n∑j=0mai,jxi∂j|ai,j∈ℂ,𝒟x0⊂𝒟, for all sing pts x0}{\mathcal{L}}(m,n,{\mathcal{D}})=\{L=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\sum_{j=0}^{m}a_{i,j}x^{i}{\partial}^{j}\ |a_{i,j}\in{\mathbb{C}},{\mathcal{D}}_{x_{0}}\subset{\mathcal{D}},\mbox{ for all sing pts }x_{0}\} is a constructible set. To describe the linear algebraic groups for which ℒ⁡(m,n,𝒟,G){\mathcal{L}}(m,n,{\mathcal{D}},G) is a constructible set, we need the following definitions.

Definition 8

Let GG a linear algebraic group defined over CC, an algebraically closed field and let G0G^{0} be the identity component.
1) A character χ\chi is a polynomial homomorphism χ:G→C∗\chi:G\rightarrow C^{*}.
2) K​e​r​X​(G0)KerX(G^{0}) is defined to be the intersection of kernels of all characters χ:G0→C∗\chi:G^{0}\rightarrow C^{*}.

Examples 9

1) If GG is finite, then K​e​r​X​(G0)KerX(G^{0}) is trivial.
2) If G0G^{0} is semisimple or unipotent, then K​e​r​X​(G0)=G0KerX(G^{0})=G^{0}.

One can show [Sin93] that K​e​r​X​(G0)KerX(G^{0}) is the smallest normal subgroup such that G0/K​e​r​X​(G0)G^{0}/KerX(G^{0}) is a torus. In addition it is the subgroup generated by all unipotent elements of G0G^{0}. Furthermore, K​e​r​X​(G0)KerX(G^{0}) is normal in GG and we have

1→G0/K​e​r​X​(G0)→G/K​e​r​X​(G0)→G/G0→11\rightarrow G^{0}/KerX(G^{0})\rightarrow G/KerX(G^{0})\rightarrow G/G^{0}\rightarrow 1

Finally, G0/K​e​r​X​(G0)G^{0}/KerX(G^{0}) is abelian, so we have that G/G0G/G^{0} acts on G0/K​e​r​X​(G0)G^{0}/KerX(G^{0}).

Theorem 10.

[Sin93] Assume that the action of G/G0G/G^{0} on G0/K​e​r​X​(G0)G^{0}/KerX(G^{0}) is trivial. Then ℒ⁡(m,n,𝒟,G){\mathcal{L}}(m,n,{\mathcal{D}},G) is constructible.

Examples 11

The groups GG that satisfy the hypothesis of this theorem include all finite groups, all connected groups and all groups that are either semisimple or unipotent. An example of a group that does not satisfy the hypothesis is the group ℂ∗⋊{1,−1}{\mathbb{C}}^{*}\rtimes\{1,-1\} where −1-1 sends cc to c−1c^{-1}.

For groups satisfying the hypothesis of this theorem we can prove a result similar to Corollary 3.

Corollary 12.

Let GG be as in Theorem 10, defined over ℚ¯\overline{{\mathbb{Q}}}. Then GG can be realized as a differential Galois group over ℚ¯​(x)\overline{{\mathbb{Q}}}(x).

Proof 7.2.

(Outline) Let GG be as in Theorem 10, defined over ℚ¯\overline{{\mathbb{Q}}}. We know that GG can be realized as the differential Galois group of a linear differential equation over ℂ⁡(x){\mathbb{C}}(x), e.g., Theorem 3. A small modification of Theorem 3 allows one to assume that the local data of such an equation is defined over ℚ¯\overline{{\mathbb{Q}}} (see [Sin93]). Therefore for some n,m,𝒟n,m,{\mathcal{D}}, ℒ⁡(m,n,𝒟,G){\mathcal{L}}(m,n,{\mathcal{D}},G) has a point in ℂ(n+1)​(m+1){{\mathbb{C}}}^{(n+1)(m+1)}. The Hilbert Nullstellensatz now implies that ℒ⁡(m,n,𝒟,G){\mathcal{L}}(m,n,{\mathcal{D}},G) has a point in ℚ¯(n+1)​(m+1)\overline{{\mathbb{Q}}}^{(n+1)(m+1)}. Therefore G⊂GLmG\subset{\rm GL}_{m} is a differential Galois gp over ℚ¯​(x)\overline{{\mathbb{Q}}}(x).

The above proof ultimately depends on analytic considerations. We again note that Harbater and Hartman [Har07a, Har07c] have given a direct algebraic proof showing all linear algebraic groups defined over ℚ¯\overline{{\mathbb{Q}}} can be realized as a differential Galois group over ℚ¯​(x)\overline{{\mathbb{Q}}}(x)..
The hypotheses of Theorem 10 are needed. In fact one can construct (see [Sin93], p. 384-385)) a two-parameter family of second order linear differential equations La,t​(Y)=0L_{a,t}(Y)=0 such that

  • •

    La,t​(Y)=0L_{a,t}(Y)=0 has 44 regular singular points 0,1,∞,a0,1,\infty,a and exponents independent of the parameters a,ta,t,

  • •

    for all values of the parameters, the differential Galois group is a subgroup of ℂ∗⋊{1,−1}{\mathbb{C}}^{*}\rtimes\{1,-1\} where −1-1 sends cc to c−1c^{-1}.

  • •

    there is an elliptic curve 𝒞:y2=f⁡(x){\mathcal{C}}:y^{2}=f(x), ff cubic with (f,f′)=1(f,f^{\prime})=1 such that if (a,y⁡(a))(a,y(a)) is a point of finite order on 𝒞{\mathcal{C}} then there exists a unique tt such that the differential Galois group of La,t​(Y)=0L_{a,t}(Y)=0 is finite and conversely, the differential Galois group being finite implies that (a,y⁡(a))(a,y(a)) is a point of finite order on 𝒞{\mathcal{C}}.

One already sees in the Lamé equation

Ln,B,e​(y)=f⁡(x)​y′′+12​f′​(x)​y′−(n⁡(n+1)​x+B)​y=0L_{n,B,e}(y)=f(x)y^{\prime\prime}+\frac{1}{2}f^{\prime}(x)y^{\prime}-(n(n+1)x+B)y=0

where f⁡(x)=4​x​(x−1)​(x−e)f(x)=4x(x-1)(x-e), that the finiteness of the differential Galois group depends on relations between the fourth singular point ee and the other parameters. For example, Brioschi showed that if n+12∈ℤ,n+\frac{1}{2}\in{\mathbb{Z}}, then there exists a P∈ℚ⁡[u,v]P\in{\mathbb{Q}}[u,v] such that Ln,B,e​(y)=0L_{n,B,e}(y)=0 has finite differential Galois group if and only if P⁡(e,B)=0P(e,B)=0. Algebraic solutions of the Lamé equation are a continuing topic of interest, see [Bal81, Bal87, Dwo90, Liţ02, Mai04, BvdW04, LvdPU05].
Finally, the results of [Sin93] have been recast and generalized in [Ber02, Ber04]. In particular the conditions of Theorem 10 are shown to be necessary and sufficient and existence and properties of moduli spaces are examined (see also Chapter 12 of [dPS03]).
Parameterized Picard-Vessiot Theory. In the previous paragraphs, I examined how differential Galois groups depend algebraically on parameters that may appear in families of differential equations. Now I will examine the differential dependence and give an introduction to [CS06] were a Galois theory is developed that measures this. To make things concrete, let us consider parameterized differential equations of the form

∂Y∂x\displaystyle\frac{\partial Y}{\partial x} =\displaystyle= A⁡(x,t1,…,tm)​YA∈gln​(ℂ⁡(x,t1,…,tm)).\displaystyle A(x,t_{1},\ldots,t_{m})Y\ \ \ \ A\in{\rm gl}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}(x,t_{1},\ldots,t_{m})). (4)

If x=x0,t1=τ1,…,tm=τmx=x_{0},t_{1}=\tau_{1},\ldots,t_{m}=\tau_{m} is a point where the entries of AA are analytic, standard existence theory yields a solution Y=(yi,j​(x,t1,…,tm)),Y=(y_{i,j}(x,t_{1},\ldots,t_{m})), with yi,jy_{i,j} analytic near x=x0,t1=τ1,…,tm=τmx=x_{0},t_{1}=\tau_{1},\ldots,t_{m}=\tau_{m}. Loosely speaking, we want to define a Galois group that is the group of transformations that preserve all algebraic relations among x,t1,…,tm,x,t_{1},\ldots,t_{m}, the yi,jy_{i,j} and the derivatives of the yi,jy_{i,j} and their derivatives with respect to all the variables x,t1,…,tmx,t_{1},\ldots,t_{m}.
To put this in an algebraic setting, we let k=ℂ⁡(x,t1,…,tm)k={\mathbb{C}}(x,t_{1},\ldots,t_{m}) be a (partial) differential field with derivations Δ={∂0,∂1,…,∂m},∂0=∂∂x,∂i=∂∂tii=1,…m\Delta=\{\partial_{0},\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{m}\},\partial_{0}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x},\ \partial_{i}=\frac{\partial}{\partial t_{i}}\ i=1,\ldots m. We let

K=k(y1,1,…,yn,n,…,∂1n1∂2n2⋯∂mnmyi,j,…)=k⟨y1,1,…,yn,n⟩Δ.K=k(y_{1,1},\ldots,y_{n,n},\ldots,\partial_{1}^{n_{1}}\partial_{2}^{n_{2}}\cdots\partial_{m}^{n_{m}}y_{i,j},\ldots)=k\langle y_{1,1},\ldots,y_{n,n}\rangle_{\Delta}.

Note that the fact that the yi,jy_{i,j} appear as entries of a solution of (4) implies that this field is stable under the derivation ∂0{\partial}_{0}. We shall define the parameterized Picard-Vessiot group (PPV-group) DGalΔ​(K/k){\rm DGal}_{\Delta}(K/k) to be the group of kk-automorphisms σ\sigma of KK that commute with all ∂i,i=0,…,m\partial_{i},\ i=0,\ldots,m.

Example 13

Let n=1,m=1,k=ℂ(x,t),Δ=Δ={∂x,∂t}n=1,m=1,k={\mathbb{C}}(x,t),\Delta=\Delta=\{\partial_{x},\partial_{t}\} and

∂y∂x=tx​y.\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}=\frac{t}{x}y.

This equation has y=xt=et​log⁡xy=x^{t}=e^{t\log x} as a solution. Differentiating with respect to tt and xx shows that K=ℂ⁡(x,t,xt,log⁡x)K={\mathbb{C}}(x,t,x^{t},\log x). Let σ∈D​G​a​lΔ​(K/k)\sigma\in DGal_{\Delta}(K/k).

Since ∂t(log⁡x)=0\partial_{t}(\log x)=0 we also have that ∂t(σ⁡(log⁡x)−log⁡x)=0\partial_{t}(\sigma(\log x)-\log x)=0.

Therefore,

DGalΔ​(K/k)\displaystyle{\rm DGal}_{\Delta}(K/k) =\displaystyle= {a∈k∗|∂xa=0,∂t(∂taa)=0}\displaystyle\{a\in k^{*}\ |\ \partial_{x}a=0,\ \partial_{t}(\frac{\partial_{t}a}{a})=0\}
=\displaystyle= {a∈k∗|∂xa=0,∂t2(a)a−(∂t(a))2=0}\displaystyle\{a\in k^{*}\ |\ \partial_{x}a=0,\ \partial_{t}^{2}(a)a-(\partial_{t}(a))^{2}=0\}

Remarks: (1) Let k0=ker∂x=ℂ(t)k_{0}=\ker{\partial}_{x}={\mathbb{C}}(t). This is a ∂t{\partial}_{t}-field. The PPV-group DGalΔ​(K/k){\rm DGal}_{\Delta}(K/k) can be identified with a certain subgroup of GL1​(k0){\rm GL}_{1}(k_{0}), that is, with a group of matrices whose entries satisfy a differential equations. This is an example of a linear differential algebraic group (to be defined more fully below).
(2) In fact, using partial fraction decompositions, one can see that

{a∈k∗|∂xa=0,∂t(∂taa)=0}=ℂ∗\{a\in k^{*}\ |\ \partial_{x}a=0,\ \partial_{t}(\frac{\partial_{t}a}{a})=0\}={\mathbb{C}}^{*}

This implies that for any σ∈DGalΔ​(K/k),σ⁡(log⁡x)=log⁡x\sigma\in{\rm DGal}_{\Delta}(K/k),\ \sigma(\log x)=\log x. If we want a Fundamental Theorem for this new Galois theory, we will want to have enough automorphisms so that any element u∈K\ku\in K\backslash k is moved by some automorphism. This is not the case here.
(3) If we specialize tt to be an element τ∈ℂ\tau\in{\mathbb{C}}, we get a linear differential equation whose monodromy group is generated by the map y↦e2​π​τ​yy\mapsto e^{2\pi\tau}y. One can think of the map y↦e2​π​t​yy\mapsto e^{2\pi t}y as the “parameterized monodromy map”. I would like to say that this map lies in the PPV-group and that this map generates a group that is, in some sense, dense in the PPV-group. We cannot do this yet.
Remarks (2) and (3) indicate that the PPV group does not have enough elements. When we considered the Picard-Vessiot theory, we insisted that the constants be algebraically closed. This guaranteed that (among other things) the differential Galois group (defined by polynomial equations) had enough elements. Since our PPV-groups will be defined by differential equations, it seems natural to require that the field of ∂0{\partial}_{0}-constants is “differentially closed”. More formally,

Definition 14

Let k0k_{0} be a differential field with derivations Δ0={∂1,…,∂m}\Delta_{0}=\{\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{m}\}. We say that k0k_{0} is differentially closed if any system of polynomial differential equations

f1​(y1,…,yn)=…=fr​(y1,…,yn)=0,g⁡(y1,…,yn)≠0f_{1}(y_{1},\ldots,y_{n})=\ldots=f_{r}(y_{1},\ldots,y_{n})=0,g(y_{1},\ldots,y_{n})\neq 0

with coefficients in k0k_{0} that has a solution in some Δ0−\Delta_{0}-differential extension field has a solution in k0k_{0}.

Differentially closed fields play the same role in differential algebra as algebraically closed fields play in algebraic geometry and share many (but not all) of the same general properties and, using Zorn’s Lemma, they are not hard to construct. They have been studied by Kolchin (under the name of constrained closed differential fields [Kol74]) and by many logicians [Mar00]. We need two more definitions before we state the main facts concerning parameterized Picard-Vessiot theory.

Definition 15

Let k0k_{0} be a differential field with derivations Δ0={∂1,…,∂m}\Delta_{0}=\{\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{m}\}.
(1) A set X⊂k0nX\subset k_{0}^{n} is Kolchin closed if it is the zero set of a system of differential polynomials over k0k_{0}.
(2) A linear differential algebraic group is a subgroup G⊂GLn​(k0)G\subset{\rm GL}_{n}(k_{0}) that is Kolchin closed in GLn​(k0)⊂k0n2{\rm GL}_{n}(k_{0})\subset k_{0}^{n^{2}}.

Kolchin closed sets form the closed sets of a topology called the Kolchin topology. I will therefore use topological language (open, dense, etc) to describe their properties. Examples and further description of linear differential algebraic groups are given after the following definition and result.

Definition 16

Let kk be a differential field with derivations Δ={∂0,∂1,…,∂m}\Delta=\{\partial_{0},\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{m}\} and let

∂0Y=A​Y,A∈gln​(k)\displaystyle\partial_{0}Y=AY,\ \ A\in{\rm gl}_{n}(k) (5)

A Parameterized Picard-Vessiot extension (PPV-extension) of kk for (5) is a Δ\Delta-ring R⊃kR\supset k such that RR is a simple Δ\Delta-ring (i.e., its only Δ\Delta-ideals are (0)(0) and RR) and RR is generated as a Δ\Delta-ring by the entries of some Z∈GLn​(R)Z\in{\rm GL}_{n}(R) and 1detZ\frac{1}{\det Z} where ∂0Z=A​Z\partial_{0}Z=AZ. A PPV-field is defined to be the quotient field of a PPV-ring.

As in the usual Picard-Vessiot theory, such rings exist and are domains. Under the assumption that k0=ker∂0k_{0}=\ker{\partial}_{0} is a differentially closed Δ0={∂1,…,∂m}\Delta_{0}=\{\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{m}\}-field, PPV-rings can be shown to be unique (up to appropriate isomorphism).

Theorem 17.

Let kk be a differential field with derivations Δ={∂0,∂1,…,∂m}\Delta=\{\partial_{0},\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{m}\} and assume that k0=ker∂0k_{0}=\ker{\partial}_{0} is a differentially closed Δ0={∂1,…,∂m}\Delta_{0}=\{\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{m}\}-field. Let KK be the PPV-field for an equation

∂0Y=A​Y,A∈gln​(k).\partial_{0}Y=AY,\ \ A\in{\rm gl}_{n}(k).

(1) The group DGalΔ​(K/k){\rm DGal}_{\Delta}(K/k) (called the PPV-group) of Δ\Delta-differential kk-automorphisms of KK has the structure of a linear differential algebraic group.
(2) There is a Galois correspondence between Δ\Delta-subfields EE of KK containing kk and Kolchin Δ0\Delta_{0} closed subgroups HH of DGalΔ​(K/k){\rm DGal}_{\Delta}(K/k) with normal subgroups HH corresponding to field KK that are again PPV-extensions of kk.

In the context of this theorem we can recast the above example. Let k0,ℂ⁡(t)⊂k0k_{0},{\mathbb{C}}(t)\subset k_{0} be a differentially closed ∂t{\partial}_{t}-field and k=k0​(x)k=k_{0}(x) be a Δ={∂x,∂t}\Delta=\{{\partial}_{x},{\partial}_{t}\} field where ∂x(k0)=0,∂x(x)=1,∂t(x)=0{\partial}_{x}(k_{0})=0,{\partial}_{x}(x)=1,{\partial}_{t}(x)=0. One can show that the field K=k<xt>Δ=k(xt,log)K=k<x^{t}>_{\Delta}=k(x^{t},\log) is a PPV-field for the equation ∂xY=tx​Y{\partial}_{x}Y=\frac{t}{x}Y with PPV group as described above. Because k0k_{0} is differentially closed, this PPV group has enough elements so that the Galois correspondence holds. Furthermore the element e2​π​i​t∈k0e^{2\pi it}\in k_{0} is an element of this group and, in fact, generates a Kolchin dense subgroup.
Remarks: (1) In general, let ∂xY=A​Y{\partial}_{x}Y=AY is a parameterized equation with A∈ℂ⁡(x,t1,…,tm)A\in{\mathbb{C}}(x,t_{1},\ldots,t_{m}). For each value of t¯\bar{t} of t=(t1,…,tm)t=(t_{1},\ldots,t_{m}) at which the entries of AA are defined and generators {γi}\{\gamma_{i}\} of the Riemann Sphere punctured at the poles of A⁡(x,t¯1,…​t¯m)A(x,\bar{t}_{1},\ldots\bar{t}_{m}), we can define monodromy matrices {Mi​(t¯)}\{M_{i}(\bar{t})\}. For all values of tt in a sufficiently small open set, the entries of MiM_{i} are analytic functions of tt and one can show that these matrices belong to the PPV-group. If the equation ∂xY=A​Y{\partial}_{x}Y=AY has only regular singular points, then one can further show that these matrices generate a Kolchin dense subgroup of the PPV group.
(2) One can consider parameterized families of linear partial differential equations as well. Let kk be a Δ={∂0,…,∂s,∂s+1,…,∂m}\Delta=\{{\partial}_{0},\ldots,{\partial}_{s},{\partial}_{s+1},\ldots,{\partial}_{m}\} and let

∂iY=AiY,Ai∈gln(k),i=0,…,s{\partial}_{i}Y=A_{i}Y,\ A_{i}\in{\rm gl}_{n}(k),\ i=0,\ldots,s

be a system of differential equations with ∂i(Aj)+Ai​Aj=∂j(Ai)+Aj​Ai{\partial}_{i}(A_{j})+A_{i}A_{j}={\partial}_{j}(A_{i})+A_{j}A_{i}. One can develop a parameterized differential Galois theory for these as well.
(3) One can develop a theory of parameterized liouvillian functions and show that one can solve parameterized linear differential in terms of these if and only if the PPV group is solvable-by-finite.
To clarify and apply the PPV theory, we will describe some facts about linear differential algebraic groups.
Linear differential algebraic groups. These groups were introduced by Cassidy [Cas72]. A general theory of differential algebraic groups was initiated by Kolchin [Kol85] and developed by Buium, Hrushovsky, Pillay, Sit and others (see [CS06] for references). We give here some examples and results. Let k0k_{0} be a differentially closed Δ0={∂1,…,∂m}\Delta_{0}=\{{\partial}_{1},\ldots,{\partial}_{m}\} differential field.

Inverse Problem. In analogy to the Picard-Vessiot theory, the question I will discuss is: Given a differential field kk, which linear differential algebraic groups appear a PPV-groups over kk? Even in simple cases the complete answer is not known and there are some surprises.
Let Δ={∂x,∂t},Δ0={∂x}\Delta=\{{\partial}_{x},{\partial}_{t}\},\Delta_{0}=\{{\partial}_{x}\}, k0k_{0} a ∂t{\partial}_{t}-differentially closed ∂t{\partial}_{t}-field and k=k0​(x)k=k_{0}(x) with ∂0(k0)=0,∂x(x)=1{\partial}_{0}(k_{0})=0,{\partial}_{x}(x)=1, an ∂t(x)=0{\partial}_{t}(x)=0. Let C⊂k0C\subset k_{0} be the Δ\Delta-cnstants of kk. I will show that all differential subgroups of Ga=(k0,+)G_{a}=(k_{0},+) appear as PPV-groups over this field but that the full group GaG_{a} does not appear as a PPV-group [CS06].
One can show that the task of describing the differential subgroups of GaG_{a} that appear as PPV-groups is equivalent to describing which linear differential algebraic groups appear as PPV-groups for equations of the form

d​yd​x=a⁡(t,x),a⁡(t,x)∈k0​(x)\frac{dy}{dx}=a(t,x),\ a(t,x)\in k_{0}(x)

Using partial fraction decomposition, one sees that a solution of such an equation is of the form

y=R(t,x)+∑i=1sai(t)log(x−bi(t)),R(t,x)∈k0(x),ai(t),bi(t)∈k0y=R(t,x)+\sum_{i=1}^{s}a_{i}(t)\log(x-b_{i}(t)),R(t,x)\in k_{0}(x),a_{i}(t),b_{i}(t)\in k_{0}

and the associated PPV-extension is of the form K=k⁡(y)K=k(y). If HH is the PPV-group of KK over kk and σ∈H\sigma\in H, then one shows that

σ⁡(y)=R⁡(t,x)+∑i=1sai​(t)​log⁡(x−bi​(t))+∑i=1sci​ai​(t)\sigma(y)=R(t,x)+\sum_{i=1}^{s}a_{i}(t)\log(x-b_{i}(t))+\sum_{i=1}^{s}c_{i}a_{i}(t)

for some ci∈Cc_{i}\in C. Let L∈k0​[dd​t]L\in k_{0}[\frac{d}{dt}] have solution space spanned by the ai​(t)a_{i}(t) (note that L≠0L\neq 0). For any σ∈H\sigma\in H, σ\sigma can be identified with an element of

H={z∈Ga(k0)|L(z)=0.}H=\{z\in G_{a}(k_{0})\ |\ L(z)=0.\}

Conversely, any element of HH can be shown to induce a differential automorphism of KK, so HH is the PPV-group. Therefore HH must be a proper subgroup of GaG_{a} and not all of GaG_{a}. One can furthermore show that all proper differential algebraic subgroups of GaG_{a} can appear in this way.
A distinguishing feature of proper subgroups of GaG_{a} is that they contain a finitely generated Kolchin dense subgroup whereas GaG_{a} does not have such a subgroup. A possible conjecture is that a linear differential algebraic group HH is a PPV-group over kk if and only if HH has a finitely generated Kolchin dense subgroup. If HH has such a finitely generated subgroup, a parameterized solution of Hilbert’s 22n​d22^{nd} shows that one can realize this group as a PPV-group. If one could establish a parameterized version of Ramis’s theorem that the formal monodromy, exponential torus and Stokes generate a a dense subgroup of the differential Galois group (something of independent interest), the other implication of this conjecture would be true.
I will now construct a field over which one can realize GaG_{a} as a PPV-group. Let kk be as above and let F=k⁡(log⁡x,xt−1​e−x)F=k(\log x,x^{t-1}e^{-x}). The incomplete Gamma function

γ⁡(t,x)=∫0xst−1​e−s​𝑑s\gamma(t,x)=\int_{0}^{x}s^{t-1}e^{-s}ds

d​γd​x=xt−1​e−x\frac{d\gamma}{dx}=x^{t-1}e^{-x}

over FF. The PPV-group over kk is Ga​(k0)G_{a}(k_{0}) because γ,d​γd​t,d2​γd​t2,…\gamma,\frac{d\gamma}{dt},\frac{d^{2}\gamma}{dt^{2}},\ldots are algebraically independent over kk [JRR95] and so there are no relations to preserve. Over k=k0​(x)k=k_{0}(x), γ⁡(t,x)\gamma(t,x) satisfies

d2​γd​x2−t−1−xx​d​γd​x=0\frac{d^{2}\gamma}{dx^{2}}-\frac{t-1-x}{x}\ \frac{d\gamma}{dx}=0

and the PPV-group is

Isomonodromic families. The parameterized Picard-Vessiot theory can be used to characterize isomonodromic families of linear differential equations with regular singular points, that is, families of such equations where the monodromy is independent of the parameters.

Definition 19

Let kk be a Δ={∂0,…,∂m}\Delta=\{{\partial}_{0},\ldots,{\partial}_{m}\}-differential field and let A∈gln​(k)A\in{\rm gl}_{n}(k). We say that ∂0Y=A​Y{\partial}_{0}Y=AY is completely integrable if there exist Ai∈gln(k),i=0,1,…,mA_{i}\in{\rm gl}_{n}(k),i=0,1,\ldots,m with A0=AA_{0}=A such that

∂jAi−∂iAj=AjAi−AiAj for all i,j=0,…m{\partial}_{j}A_{i}-{\partial}_{i}A_{j}=A_{j}A_{i}-A_{i}A_{j}\mbox{ for all }i,j=0,\ldots m

The nomenclature is motivated by the fact that the latter conditions on the AiA_{i} are the usual integrability conditions on the system of differential equations ∂iY=AY,i=,…,m{\partial}_{i}Y=AY,i=,\ldots,m.

Proposition 20.

[CS06] Let kk be a Δ={∂0,…,∂m}\Delta=\{{\partial}_{0},\ldots,{\partial}_{m}\}-differential field and let A∈gln​(k)A\in{\rm gl}_{n}(k). Assume that k0=ker∂0k_{0}=\ker{\partial}_{0} is Δ0={∂1,…,∂m}\Delta_{0}=\{{\partial}_{1},\ldots,{\partial}_{m}\}-differentially closed field and let KK be the PPV-field of kk for ∂0Y=A​Y{\partial}_{0}Y=AY with A∈gln​(k)A\in{\rm gl}_{n}(k). Let C=∩i=0mker∂iC=\cap_{i=0}^{m}\ker{\partial}_{i}.
There exists a linear algebraic group GG, defined over CC, such that
DGalΔ​(K/k){\rm DGal}_{\Delta}(K/k) is conjugate to G⁡(C)G(C) over k0k_{0} if and only if ∂0Y=A​Y{\partial}_{0}Y=AY is completely integrable. If this is the case, then KK is a Picard-Vessiot extension corresponding to this integrable system.

Let k=ℂ⁡(x,t1,…,tn)k={\mathbb{C}}(x,t_{1},\ldots,t_{n}) and A∈gln​(k)A\in{\rm gl}_{n}(k). For t=(t1,…,tm)t=(t_{1},\ldots,t_{m}) in some sufficiently small open set 𝒪⊂ℂn{\mathcal{O}}\subset{\mathbb{C}}^{n}, one can select generators {γi​(ti,…,tm)}\{\gamma_{i}(t_{i},\ldots,t_{m})\} of the fundamental group of the Riemann Sphere minus the (parameterized) singular points such that the monodromy matrices {Mi​(t1,…,tm)}\{M_{i}(t_{1},\ldots,t_{m})\} depend analytically on the parameters. One says that the differential equation ∂xY=A​Y{\partial}_{x}Y=AY is isomonodromic if for some sufficiently small open set 𝒪{\mathcal{O}}, the MiM_{i} are independent of tt. In [CS06] we deduce the following corollary from the above result.

Corollary 21.

Let k,A,𝒪k,A,{\mathcal{O}} be as above and assume that ∂xY=A​Y{\partial}_{x}Y=AY has only regular singular points for t∈𝒪t\in{\mathcal{O}}. Then ∂xY=A​Y{\partial}_{x}Y=AY is isomonodromic if and only if the PPV-group is conjugate to a linear algebraic group G​(ℂ)⊂GLn​(ℂ).G({\mathbb{C}})\subset{\rm GL}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}).

Second order parameterized equations. A classification of the linear differential subgroups of SL2{\rm SL}_{2} allows one to classify parameterized systems of second order linear differential equations. To simplify the discussion we will consider equations of the form

∂Y∂x=A⁡(x,t)​Y\frac{{\partial}Y}{{\partial}x}=A(x,t)Y

that depend on only one parameter and satisfy A∈sln​(ℂ⁡(x,t))A\in{\rm sl}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}(x,t)).
Let HH be a linear differential algebraic subgroup of SL2​(k0){\rm SL}_{2}(k_{0}) (where k0k_{0} is a ∂t{\partial}_{t}-differentially closed field containing ℂ⁡(t){\mathbb{C}}(t) and ker∂t=ℂ\ker{\partial}_{t}={\mathbb{C}}) and H¯\bar{H} its Zariski closure. If H¯≠SL2\bar{H}\neq{\rm SL}_{2}, then one can show that H¯\bar{H} and therefore HH is solvable-by-finite [Kov86, Cas72]. Furthermore, Cassidy’s result (Example 18(3)) states that if H¯=SL2\bar{H}={\rm SL}_{2} but H≠SL2H\neq{\rm SL}_{2}, then HH is conjugate to SL2​(ℂ){\rm SL}_{2}({\mathbb{C}}). From this discussion and the discussion in the previous paragraphs one can conclude the following.

Proposition 22.

Let kk and ∂Y∂x=A​Y\frac{{\partial}Y}{{\partial}x}=AY be as above. Assume that for some small open set of values of tt that this equation has only regular singular points. Then either

  • •

    the PPV group is SL2{\rm SL}_{2}, or

  • •

    the equation is solvable in terms of parameterized exponentials, integrals and algebraics, or

  • •

    the equation is isomonodromic.

The notion of ‘solvable in terms of parameterized exponentials, integrals and algebraics’ is analogous to the similar notion in the usual Picard-Vessiot theory and is given a formal definition in [CS06], where it is also shown that this notion is equivalent to the PPV-group being solvable-by-finite.

8 Final Comments

I have touched on only a few of the aspects of the Galois theory of linear differential equations. I will indicate here some of the other aspects and give pointers to some of the current literature.
Kolchin himself generalized this theory to a theory of strongly normal extension fields [Kol76]. The Galois groups in this theory are arbitrary algebraic groups for which Kolchin. Recently Kovacic [Kov03, Kov06] has recast this theory in terms of groups schemes and differential schemes. Umemura [Ume90, Ume96b, Ume96a, Ume99, Ume, Ume04] has developed a Galois theory of differential equations for general nonlinear equation. Instead of Galois groups, Umemura uses Lie algebras to measure the symmetries of differential fields. Malgrange [Mal02, Mal01] has proposed a Galois theory of differential equations where the role of the Galois group is replaced by certain groupoids. This theory has been expanded and applied by Cassale [Cas06a, Cas06b, Cas07]. Pillay [Pil97, Pil98, MP97, Pil02, Pil04] develops a Galois theory where the Galois groups can be arbitrary differential algebraic groups and, together with Bertrand, has used these techniques to generalize Ax’s work on Schanuel’s conjecture (see [Ber07, Ber06]). Landesman [Lan06] has generalized Kolchin’s theory of strongly normal extension to a theory of strongly normal parameterized extensions. The theory of Cassidy and myself presented in Section 7 can be viewed as a special case of this theory and many of the results of [CS06] can be derived from the theories of Umemura and Malgrange as well.
A Galois Theory of linear difference equations has also been developed, initally by Franke ([Fra63] and several subsequent papers), Bialynicki-Birula [BB62] and more fully by van der Put and myself [dPS97]. André [And01] has presented a Galois theory that treats both the difference and differential case in a way that allows one to see the differential case as a limit of the difference case. Chatzidakis, Hrushovski and Kamensky have used model theoretic tools to develop Galois theory of difference equations (see [CH99], [Kam06] and [CHS07] for a discussion of connections with the other theories). Algorithmic issues have been considered by Abramov, Barkatou, Bronstein, Hendriks, van Hoeij, Kauers, Petkovsek, Paule, Schneider, Wilf, M. Wu and Zeilberger and there is an extensive literature on the subject for which I will refer to MathSciNet and the ArXiV. Recently work by André, Di Vizio, Etingof, Hardouin, van der Put, Ramis, Reversat, Sauloy, and Zhang, has been done on understanding the Galois theory of qq-difference equation (see [DV02, DV04, ADV04, Eti95, dPR07, Sau03, RS07, RSZ06, DVRSZ03, Ram07, Har07b]). Fields with both derivations and automorphisms have been studied from a model theoretic point of view by Bustamente [Med05] and work of Abramov, Bronstein, Li, Petkovsek, Wu, Zheng and myself [AP94, ABP95, BP96, BP94, BLW05, LSWZ06, Wu05] consider algorithmic questions for mixed differential-difference systems. The Picard-Vessiot theory of linear differential equations has been used by Hardouin [Har06] to study the differential properties of solutions of difference equations. A Galois theory, with linear differential algebraic groups as Galois groups, designed to measure the differential relations among solutions of difference equation, has been recently developed and announced in [Sin07].
Finally, I have not touched on the results and enormous literature concerning the hypergeometric equations and their generalizations as well as arithmetic properties of differential equations. For a taste of the current research, I refer the reader to [SST00] and [HUY07] for the former and [ABB04] for the latter.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
